papers.title: How DiamondEdge Actually Works
papers.subtitle: Four analysts who never read the same stats, a strategy that gets rebuilt every single night, and a set of rules that stop us fooling ourselves — and stop us fooling you.
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
Most sports models are sold to you as a number: 60% winners, look at the backtest. This paper is the opposite of that. It explains exactly how DiamondEdge is built, what it has actually done, and — the part almost nobody publishes — what we have proven it *cannot* do.

The system is four analysts who genuinely disagree because they are looking at genuinely different things, a strategy layer that picks a fresh playbook every single night from about 2,800 candidates, a training rule that means no model is ever graded on a game it was allowed to study first, and a set of rails that will refuse to grade a game at all if two independent sources disagree about the final score.

The honest headline: that nightly process has won 54.8% on 997 picks across 205 nights, +45.4 units at standard juice, against a 52.4% break-even. The honest asterisk, which we print in the same size: the error bars on that still reach below zero, so it is a process that has been winning rather than a proven edge — and we serve it that way.

We also measured the ceiling. Across five seasons and 8,412 games, the best hit rate achievable by *any* rule, including free ones, is 52.1%, and it belongs to the market. That is why we do not promise you 60%.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### Four analysts who never read the same stats

The desk is four characters, and they are not four skins on one model. Each one owns a different slice of the game, and no two of them can see the same number.

- **SCOUT — the arms.** Both starting pitchers and both bullpens. Bad pitching means runs.
- **NOVA — the bats.** The nine names actually posted tonight, against the hand they will face, plus how the two offences have really been scoring.
- **ATLAS — the conditions.** The ballpark, the altitude, the roof, day or night, and how many runs this plate umpire's games actually produce.
- **VEGA — the price.** Where the number opened, how far it moved, how much the books disagree, and what each side actually costs.

The split is enforced by the code, not by good intentions. Across 613 different stats, the four slices do not overlap on a single one — hand an analyst a stat that belongs to somebody else and the program stops with an error.

There is a reason this is so strict, and it is embarrassing enough that we published it: the old version of the desk *did* have four analysts, and they were all secretly reading the same thing. All four hit between 48.6% and 51.0%. We ran a check across 357 different ways of slicing their performance looking for any real specialty, and found zero. Four analysts who agree because they are looking at the same data are not a desk. They are one opinion with four faces.

### Nobody uses a black box

Each analyst is a short list of readable factors with one published weight each. You can recompute any read on paper — there is literally a command that prints every multiplication.

Each factor also has its direction locked in advance, because baseball physics is not up for debate. Worse pitching means more runs. When we first fitted this without that lock, the math produced "worse starters mean *fewer* runs" — which is not a discovery, it is a warning light. Now, if a factor's data points the wrong way, its weight is set to exactly zero and the read says so out loud.

### The strategy is rebuilt every night

Here is the part that is genuinely unusual. We do not hunt for one strategy that always works. We built about 2,848 different ways of turning the desk's voices into a pick — follow one analyst, take the majority, weight them, only bet certain totals, only bet when the number moved, sit out when they disagree, and the exact reverse of all of it.

Then every night, we check how each of those 2,848 has actually been doing over the last five weeks, take the 21 that have been running best, let them vote, and play the majority side tomorrow. Tomorrow it happens again with fresh numbers.

The strategy that gets played is disposable. It lives one day and is judged on a day it never saw.

### No rewinding the tape

Every number in this system comes from a model that could actually have existed on the morning of the game. The rule is one line: to predict a given day, train only on games that had already finished before it.

That sounds obvious. It is also the single most common way published sports records lie, because it is very easy to accidentally let tomorrow's information into yesterday's model. So we do not just intend it — a check runs on every single night's data and *stops the program* if the window it used to pick tonight's strategy includes tonight.

Building the honest replay this way required training 5,894 separate models. That is the cost, and it is why our numbers are smaller than the ones you see elsewhere.

### The rails

Three rules stand between the research and what you see.

**The price has to have existed.** A price we show has to be for the exact total we picked, in the full-game market, live at the moment we decided, from a book that was actually posting right then. If no such price exists, the game shows as unpriceable and cannot become a pick. It does not quietly get paid at the next best number.

**Two sources have to agree on the score.** Grading used to read finals from one place. Now it also checks a genuinely separate newsroom, and if they disagree, the game is not graded — not dropped, not guessed. It sits on the board until they agree.

**Nothing gets rewritten.** A graded pick is frozen forever. When we find a mistake, we publish the mistake. We do not go back and edit the record.

### AI, and where it is deliberately locked out

The system runs current-generation AI in three real places: models retrain themselves every night on everything graded so far; each analyst gets an AI session that reads its own slice and writes a short note; and multi-agent AI pipelines mine our own past failures for ideas nobody had thought to test.

What AI never does is pick a side, set a probability, move a stake, or touch a record. That is not a promise about intent — those fields are written and locked *before* any AI session runs. We test it adversarially: an AI response that tries to set the pick side, the probability, the star rating and the result leaves the board byte-for-byte identical. That is a test that runs, not a policy we wrote down.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
### The record, with the asterisk attached

Replayed under the strict no-rewinding rule, the nightly process played 205 of 235 available nights and 997 picks at **54.8%**, returning **+45.4 units** at standard juice — a 4.6% return, with a worst losing stretch of 11.3 units.

Break-even at standard juice is 52.4%. So 54.8% is 2.4 points clear of it.

And the honest part: the range around that number still reaches slightly below zero. A run like this could still be luck. We say so on the page, and the code that serves it has a built-in test that *fails* if anyone ever publishes it without the range attached.

### The control that makes it interesting

The obvious objection is that picking a strategy each night is just noise dressed up. So we ran exactly the same machinery, but picked the nightly strategy *at random* out of the same bag. Forty different attempts.

Random selection lost an average of **93.4 units**. The best of the forty still lost 5.8. Our selection made +43.9 on the same stretch. The gap is about three and a half standard deviations. The nightly choosing is doing real work.

### Three things we found that we would rather not have

**The market is very good.** We built seven different models — simple ones, a 98-stat machine-learning model, a full physics simulator — and scored them all on the same 8,412 games. The best got 51.5%, which is not statistically better than just betting the under every night. The single best thing anyone could do, of any kind, was copy the market's own side at 52.1%. That is under the 52.4% break-even. The market is not beatable on this bet by us, and probably not by anyone, and we published the whole study.

**One analyst alone is not an edge.** Over their first 331 graded reads each: VEGA 50.9%, NOVA 48.8%, SCOUT 46.6%, ATLAS 43.2%. We publish those and claim nothing from them. At 331 picks the error bar is about ±5.4 points — wider than any edge worth having. A number below 50% is no more a finding than one above it.

**We caught ourselves betting the market's own number back at it.** This is the most important thing we have found, and it has its own paper. Three of our four analysts were supposed to be betting their own read of the game. It turned out the thing they were betting was 51% correlated with the posted total — the market's number already contained most of what the analyst thought was its own contribution. Their records were partly just a bet on which way the month's totals happened to fall.

We rebuilt them so their signal is genuinely independent of the price. On the same 374 games, ATLAS went from 88% mixed up with the line and hitting 44.26%, to essentially independent and hitting 49.73%. Same analyst, same information, same games — the difference is that it stopped betting the market's number.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
In a market this sharp, the ordinary way to fail is not being wrong. It is being *convincingly* wrong.

Almost anything looks like an edge on a few hundred games. We have proven this on ourselves, on purpose, four separate times. The cleanest demonstration: in our strategy search, 98 candidates passed every quality check on the discovery data at an average 59.95% hit rate and +14.4% return. We then ran those exact 98 forward onto games they had not seen. They averaged **−32.3%**. Not one was positive. Ninety-four went the other way entirely.

That is the environment. A system that cannot tell a real 55% from a lucky 55% is worse than useless in it, because it will confidently sell you the lucky one.

Everything expensive about how DiamondEdge is built — writing down what we are testing before we test it, sealing off data we are not allowed to look at, running the math that catches lucky-looking results, grading by nights instead of by picks, throwing away our best single bet and checking the result still holds, recomputing predictions by hand to make sure the code does what we say — buys exactly one thing. The ability to tell those two apart.

Which leads to the reason we publish our failures. We have tested roughly seventy different ideas for beating this market and closed most of them as dead, with the numbers attached, including several that looked spectacular right up until they were tested properly. That is not modesty. It is the only evidence you have that the things we *do* claim were not picked the same way.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
Every pick you see went through this: a strategy chosen using only nights that had already been graded, applied to a game, at a price that genuinely existed at that moment, on a total a book actually posted, graded later against a final score that two independent sources agreed on.

The confidence next to it comes from readable factors you could recompute yourself, not from a black box. When an analyst has thin information — say the plate umpire has not been assigned yet — the card tells you, its conviction is scaled down automatically, and it is not allowed to write a sentence claiming it read something it did not.

And what you will *not* see matters just as much. We do not claim to beat the closing line. We tested that claim about sixty-five different ways with pre-registered honest methods, and it is false for us in every market we can measure. What we claim is a process with a public record that started the day it went live, a price gate that has never been loosened by a basis point, and an error bar printed next to every number.

When that record earns a range that clears zero, you will see the range too.

papers.title: Why Our Four Analysts Never Read the Same Stats
papers.subtitle: We had four analysts who agreed almost every time. It turned out they were all secretly reading the same thing. Here is how we caught it, and what we rebuilt.
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
A desk of analysts is only worth showing you if the analysts genuinely disagree. Ours did not.

We checked. All four were hitting between 48.6% and 51.0%. We looked for any real specialty across 357 different slices of their performance and found exactly zero. And across 2,972 games, whether they agreed unanimously, split down the middle, or three-against-one made no difference to how often they were right. Four analysts who look at the same data are not four opinions. They are one opinion wearing four name tags.

So we rebuilt them. Each analyst now owns a completely separate set of stats — 613 columns, split four ways, with zero overlap and code that refuses to break the rule. And we changed *what they bet*: instead of comparing their projection to the posted total, each one now bets whether its own channel says this game is above or below an average game.

That second change is the one that mattered. It moved how often two analysts pick the same side from 84–89% down to 51–57%.

What we are *not* claiming: that this makes them profitable. It does not, on the evidence so far, and we publish their records to prove we are not pretending otherwise.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### The measurement that forced a rebuild

Three findings, and together they were damning.

Every analyst's hit rate sat between 48.6% and 51.0% — a coin flip with rounding. A sweep across 357 different performance slices, with the math applied that catches lucky-looking results, found no real specialty anywhere. And no consensus configuration separated from chance.

That last one is worth explaining, because it is the check people usually skip. The obvious question about a four-analyst desk is: *when they all agree, is that a stronger signal?* We could only test that on 325 games at first, which is nowhere near enough. So we went and rebuilt one analyst's history back across two extra seasons — properly, with a hard seal so it could never touch data it was not allowed to see — taking the sample from **325 games to 2,972**.

The answer came back clean and disappointing:

| Desk state | Games | Hit rate | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| All four agree | 459 | 47.3% | 42.6% – 52.0% |
| Three against one | 1,517 | 50.6% | 48.0% – 53.1% |
| Split two-two | 996 | 50.0% | 46.9% – 53.1% |

Not one result in that entire table — three families, four dissenters, six split pairs, six head-to-heads — clears a coin flip.

And the small-sample version that had looked exciting? It was 14 wins in 34 unanimous games. On the deepened data, that is exactly what a 47.8% process produces. The odds of seeing it by chance: a dead 50/50.

### Four genuinely different jobs

The rebuild gave each analyst one causal channel of a baseball total, and nothing else.

**SCOUT — the arms.** *Runs come from bad pitching, so I grade the arms and nothing else: the two starters who open the game and the bullpens behind them. Weak staffs mean runs, and I lean over.*

**NOVA — the bats.** *Runs come from bats, so I grade the hitters and nothing else: the nine names actually posted tonight against the hand they will face, and how the two offences have really been scoring.*

**ATLAS — the conditions.** *Runs are a physical event, so I grade the place and the man behind the plate: the park's run factor, its altitude and roof, day or night, and how many runs this umpire's games actually produce.*

**VEGA — the price.** *The number is the evidence: where it opened, how far it moved, how much the books disagree, and what the two sides actually cost.*

The split is enforced in code. Try to hand an analyst a stat from someone else's slice and the program stops.

A few of the exclusions are worth knowing about, because they are where a split like this usually leaks.

*Umpire over-rates* — the share of a ref's games that went over the closing total — sound like ATLAS's business. They are not. They measure the *market's* number, so putting them in ATLAS would smuggle the price into the conditions channel and quietly re-connect ATLAS to VEGA. ATLAS reads umpires through raw runs, strikeouts and walks against a league baseline instead.

*Weather* is excluded, and this one is a coverage problem rather than a purity one. Our weather data goes from about 98% complete in 2022–2024 to **35.6% in 2025 and 0.6% in 2026**, and what remains is an after-the-fact archive product our own rules exclude. The brief asked for park and weather. The honest half of that is what shipped, and it says so on the page rather than quietly filling in the gaps.

### Nothing fitted backwards

Each analyst is a handful of readable factors with one published weight each — no black box. You can recompute any read by hand.

Every factor's direction is locked in advance to known baseball physics. The reason is a real failure we hit: the factors inside one analyst overlap heavily (a starter's ERA, his recent form and the expected damage against him are three views of the same arm), and when you fit overlapping inputs without a lock, the math flips signs to fit noise. Our first attempt produced "worse starters mean **fewer** runs." That is not a finding, it is a symptom.

Now, if a factor's data points against physics, its weight is driven to exactly zero and published as *refused by the data* — never fitted backwards.

### The change that actually fixed it

Originally, each analyst compared its own projected total to the posted line. Here is what that produced:

| | how different their projections were | how often they picked the same side |
|---|---|---|
| projection vs. the posted line | well separated (0.23–0.34) | **84% – 89%** |
| betting their own deviation | — | **51% – 57%** |

The reason is arithmetic, and once you see it you cannot unsee it. An analyst built from a quarter of the information produces a projection that moves about **0.3 runs** game to game. The posted total moves **1.12 runs**. So when you compare the two, the posted total wins every argument — all three analysts lean over on low totals together and under on high totals together. Four correlated coin flips again.

Betting the deviation removes the line from the side decision entirely. Each analyst answers only its own question: *does MY channel say this game is above or below an average game, and by how much?*

"Average game" means average *right now*, not average across the training data. The centre for a given date is that analyst's own average over the previous 30 days, and only days that had already happened. Using the static training average instead, NOVA ran **79% over** in July — offences run hotter in July than the training median, and NOVA cannot see the line that prices that seasonality. With the rolling centre it runs 54%.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
**The split holds.** Verified across all 613 columns. A test also checks that all four records carry exactly the same fields, so no analyst can be shown to you on friendlier terms than another.

**The disagreement holds.** Same-side agreement fell from 84–89% to 51–57%. A separate, later campaign measured average pairwise agreement across the desk independently and got the same picture.

**Nothing leaked.** Training stops at 2026-06-30; records start 2026-07-01. That fence is proved four ways, and one of them is unusually strong: we physically chopped the source data at the fence *before any joining happened*, refitted every analyst from scratch, and required the weights to come out identical to nine decimal places. A single leaked training game would move a weight far more than that.

**The records are published and nothing is claimed from them.** First 331 graded reads each: VEGA 50.9%, NOVA 48.8%, SCOUT 46.6%, ATLAS 43.2%. No analyst shows a positive edge and none is claimed. At 331 picks the error bar is about ±5.4 points, wider than any edge worth having.

**The combiner can now fit weights, and refuses to.** Once 311 graded games had accumulated, we could finally fit a custom weight for each analyst instead of weighting them equally. The fitted weights came out at −0.016, −0.035, −0.028 and −0.061 — every single one smaller than its own margin of error. And when tested forward, the fitted version was no better than equal weighting. So equal weighting stays. A planted-signal test confirms the machinery *would* detect real weights if they existed, which is what lets this open later on evidence rather than on somebody changing their mind.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
Three things here generalise well past baseball.

**Descriptions do not create disagreement.** Before the rebuild, the four analysts had four distinct *descriptions* and one identical *information set*. Descriptions decorrelate nothing. What fixed it was a registry, a gate that errors out, and a measured check across the real data.

**Whatever moves most decides the answer.** This is the subtle one, and it is the most likely to recur anywhere else. Each analyst's projection was genuinely independent of the others. It was the *comparison to the line* that collapsed them, because the line's variation dwarfed theirs. Any system that compares a small private estimate to a big public number is really just betting the big public number. Chasing that observation further turned into the single most important market finding this program has produced, and it has its own paper.

**An empty chair beats a fake opinion — but a real read beats both.** An older version of the desk manufactured a filler read whenever an analyst had nothing, guaranteeing a full board by construction. That is a fabricated opinion presented as an opinion, and it is retired. What replaced it: the analyst files on the factors it actually has, a missing factor is set to neutral so it contributes exactly zero, and the read publishes how complete it was. On a recent slate, **236 of 236 analyst slots filed a side**, and a fully informed read comes out bit-for-bit identical to what the engine produced before any of this existed — 45 of 45 complete reads reprice exactly.

There is also a governance story worth telling, because it is the kind of thing that normally stays private. When we replaced the analysts, one module kept feeding a table built on the *old* four models into a lookup that had already been rebuilt on the new four. It never showed a wrong sentence — but only because nothing in that table survives our statistical correction, so it always returned nothing. That is luck, not safety. The module now refuses any entry that is not stamped with the new source, a lock that cannot be worked around however it is wired, and it fails to silence rather than to a number.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
When the desk shows you four opinions on a game, those are now genuinely four opinions. SCOUT is reading the arms and only the arms. ATLAS is reading the ballpark and the plate umpire and literally cannot see the price. When they disagree, that disagreement is about the game — not four models tripping over the same number.

Two honesty features come straight out of this and you will see both.

Every analyst files on every game at every point in the day, and each read tells you how much of its own information it actually had. A thin read looks thin instead of looking confident.

And a call is never a bet. The desk having a view on a game, and the price being good enough to bet, are two separate things with two separate fields — and the price gate is untouched. On one recent board that meant 15 games where the desk had a view but no bet, 3 leans and 2 plays. The old single field would have shown 15 silent "AVOID" cards on games the desk had a real opinion about.

papers.abstract:
Search a few thousand strategies over a few thousand games and you will find a winner. The winner is usually luck.

We proved that on ourselves, deliberately. Ninety-eight strategies cleared every single quality check on the data we found them on, averaging 59.95% and a +14.4% return. Run those exact ninety-eight forward onto nights they had not seen, and they averaged **−32.3%**. Not one stayed positive. Ninety-four went the other way entirely.

So we stopped looking for the strategy and started testing the *process*. Every night: score all 2,848 candidates on how they have actually been doing over the last five weeks, take the twenty-one that are running best, let them vote, play the majority side tomorrow, grade it, roll the window forward.

That process, replayed under strict no-rewinding rules, played 997 picks across 205 nights at **54.8%** — +45.4 units at standard juice, against a 52.4% break-even. And the control that makes it interesting: run identical machinery but pick the nightly strategy *at random* out of the same bag, and it loses 93.4 units on average across forty tries.

The honest asterisk, printed at the same size: the range around that +45.4 still reaches below zero. This is a process that has been winning. It is not yet a proven edge, and the code that serves it has a built-in test that fails if anyone publishes the number without the range.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### We wrote down what we expected first — and we expected to fail

Before a single strategy was scored, the rules were committed to the repository with a timestamp. Written into them, in advance: *the expected outcome is that nothing survives.*

That is not false modesty. The rules list four times this program has already watched itself find a fake edge: a table of 41 desk-agreement patterns where nothing survived checking, across 2,972 games; a leaderboard of ten prospect models whose two "significant" entries pointed in opposite directions; a candidate that looked promising and turned out untestable; and a pricing bug that manufactured an edge out of nothing.

The rules also name what they were replacing. The old adaptive system searched five lookback windows and would trust a strategy after **six** decided games. At six games, the honest range around a hit rate is about ±25 points. A "must be above 53%" filter at that sample size is not a filter. It is a rounding error with a threshold attached.

### The panel

2,860 graded games across 235 nights, from July 2025 through August 2026, carrying **29 signals per game**: the four desk analysts read at five different points in the day, plus nine research prospects, plus a market reference block (the line, the de-vigged price, how many books are posting, how much they disagree, how far the number moved).

For everything before the training cutoff, those signals were regenerated honestly — **5,894 separate model fits**, each one trained only on games that had already finished. After the cutoff, the panel uses the actual shipped reads.

Everything is scored at flat standard juice, and there is a specific reason. Reconstructing what price we *would* have got at a wall is exactly the kind of thing that inflated 34 of 58 served picks in July when we tried it elsewhere. So the tournament does not do it. Break-even is 52.38%, and no number in that whole report may be quoted as an estimate of what you would actually have made.

### The one rule that makes it honest

The strategy played on a given night is chosen using only nights strictly before it. That is checked in code — on the row numbers *and* on the real dates — and it stops the program rather than logging a warning.

That rail is what makes the whole design work, and it is worth spelling out why. Overfitting the last five weeks cannot inflate the record, because an overfit choice simply loses tomorrow and the record eats it honestly. There is no way to cheat forward.

### We planted a fake signal to make sure it works

Before trusting any of this on real data, we planted one: a signal source that is a pure coin flip for 60 nights and then 70% correct for the next 60.

The selector found it. It played strategies reading that source on **100% of the late nights** against 21% of the early ones, and earned 58.2% from it. Then we shuffled the outcomes so no signal existed, and it earned 50.8% — which is nothing. It detects a real regime and does not invent one.

### How we chose the settings — without using a leaderboard

Choosing happened on the first nine months. Two later stretches were held back and never looked at.

We also declared a product constraint *before* choosing: whatever we pick has to play at least 70% of available nights with at least two picks. That knocked the field from 2,089 candidate configurations down to 1,185 that were usable at all.

Then we deliberately did **not** take the leaderboard leader, and the reason is recorded. At one point in the search, the top configuration on the selection window returned +16.7 units on the unseen months. We then widened the search — and the *new* leader returned +0.4 units on the same unseen months. A leaderboard top is a lucky stretch wearing a crown.

So the recommendation was read off **axis medians** instead: for each setting (how far to look back, how many strategies to play, how strict to be), the median result across every single configuration that used it. That is much harder for one hot stretch to move.

We tried one more method and recorded it as rejected: taking the most common setting among the top 25. That produced a 21-night window with almost no sample requirement, which played only 58 of 235 nights, made 80 picks total, and lost. A most-common-setting-per-axis is not a configuration — it is a summary of several, and it can name one nobody actually tested.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
### The settings, and what they teach

| setting | best | worst |
|---|---|---|
| how far back to look | **35 nights** (+13.5) | 14 nights (−50.2) |
| minimum sample | **30 decided picks** (+16.4) | 250 picks (−67) |
| how many to play | **top 21** (+17.6) | top 1 (−4.6) |
| nudge toward yesterday | on (+11.7 to +20.3) | off (−2.8) |
| require consistency | on (+5.5) | off (−9.3) |
| size of the pool | wide (−3 to −4) | narrow (−48 to −56) |

Two of these are real lessons rather than dial settings.

**Look back about five weeks, not one.** Long windows beat short ones by fifty units of median, and a two-week window is among the worst settings we measured. Whatever it is that makes some strategies run better than others has staying power measured in weeks, not days.

**Keep the pool huge.** The narrow pools — "just the four analysts," "just the simple rules" — median **−48 and −56 units**, far worse than the wide ones. A narrow pool has nothing to choose between. Richness is what gives the selection something to do.

### The recommendation, in full

```
pool         every strategy we built  (2,848)
lookback     35 nights, always ending before the night being played
ranking      average profit per decided pick at standard juice
minimum      at least 30 decided picks inside that window
consistency  also profitable over the recent half AND the earlier half
play         the top 21 vote; majority side plays; a tie sits out
stickiness   a small bonus to yesterday's choice, to stop pointless churn
stake        flat, one unit per game
```

### The record

| stretch | nights | picks | hit | units | return | worst stretch | 90% range |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jul 2025 – Mar 2026 *(chosen on)* | 92 | 478 | 54.8% | +22.2 | +4.6% | 11.3 | −3.2% to +12.3% |
| Apr – Jun 2026 *(never seen)* | 85 | 383 | 55.4% | +21.7 | +5.7% | 7.6 | −1.0% to +12.7% |
| Jul – Aug 2026 *(never seen)* | 28 | 136 | 52.9% | +1.5 | +1.1% | 5.0 | −11.6% to +14.0% |
| **all played nights** | **205 of 235** | **997** | **54.8%** | **+45.4** | **+4.6%** | **11.3** | **−0.4% to +9.5%** |

It uses 461 different strategies across the replay and changes its mind on 91% of nights. About five picks a night, on roughly 87% of available nights.

### The controls

| what | units |
|---|---|
| the nightly selection | **+43.9** |
| same machinery, strategy picked at random (40 seeds) | mean **−93.4**, best seed still −5.8 |
| one fixed strategy every night | −34.4 |
| bet the under / over every game | −126.0 / −89.7 |

The random control does about 130 units worse. That gap is 3.4 standard deviations.

And the selection genuinely transfers rather than just fitting: across all 2,089 configurations, the correlation between how they did on the first stretch and the second is +0.33 — and the 25 configurations chosen on the first stretch averaged **+15.8 units** on the second, against +9.5 for the field.

### There is no hidden star in the pool

Worth being blunt about. Every one of the 29 signals, taken on its own over 2,373 games, hits between **48.2% and 51.3%**. Every single one of them loses money at standard juice. On forecast accuracy, the desk's plain equal-weight blend scores marginally *worse* than the de-vigged market and marginally worse than just saying 50% every time.

The value, if there is any, is entirely in the choosing.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
What the nightly selection exploits is not a permanent edge in any strategy. It is that at any given moment some strategies are running better than others, and that state sticks around long enough — about five weeks — to be worth following. The planted-signal test is the cleanest evidence for that reading, and the lookback results agree with it.

We also published three of our own mistakes from this campaign rather than quietly fixing them, because a research process that only shows you its clean runs is not a research process.

A loader checked a window name with a prefix match, so a variant named "power" silently fell through and both windows loaded the same 374 rows. The tell was a leaderboard where every entry had at most 29 days on a window that covers 206 nights. That whole run was voided and never reported.

A transfer study first measured its correlation over the top 200 configurations and reported **−0.63** — which looks alarming and is a classic statistical trap: if you only look at the winners overall, their components will always appear to trade off against each other. Over all configurations, the real number is **+0.37**.

A mutation bug let a four-weight recipe land on a three-source blend. The function now errors out.

One more thing we withdrew: the run-line arm. "Always take the +1.5 underdog" scores a +13.5% return on 2,411 games at a flat-juice convention, which sounds fantastic. Then we looked at the actual prices. **21.9% of run-line rows carry a two-sided price that adds up to less than 100%** — with the bottom 5% at 0.729, which would be a 37% guaranteed arbitrage on one row in twenty. That is not a market. That is a mismatched or stale quote pair. After filtering to prices that genuinely existed, exactly **43 usable run-line rows over 3 nights** survive in the whole corpus. The candidates were still generated, still scored and still counted against us in the statistical correction, stamped NOT EVALUABLE. You do not get to shrink a search by throwing away the tests that failed.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
This is the machinery behind the board. Each morning one voting ensemble is chosen from the full pool using only nights that have already been graded, and only the games it fires on become picks.

Two things you will notice, both deliberate.

**The board and the archive disagree every day, on purpose.** The board shows what today's chosen strategy fires on. The archive holds every pick ever served — never deleted, never edited, fingerprinted day by day. They are different objects and they are checked by different rails. The board is checked against the desk's own ledger, which is *stricter* than the old check because it catches a pick shown on the **wrong side**, something a count-only check could never see.

**The claim is sized to the evidence.** +45.4 units over 205 nights is a process that has been winning. The range still reaches below zero, so it is served activation-dated, graded in public from day one, with the price gate untouched — and the module ships with a test that *fails* if the published range's lower bound is ever positive. Nobody can quietly round the uncertainty away.

---

papers.title: Why the Desk Has an Opinion at 9am and a Better One at 3pm
papers.subtitle: A game eight hours out shouldn't show a blank card. But it also shouldn't show a made-up one. So we built a separate model for every analyst at every point in the day.
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
A desk that only prices games three hours before first pitch is a blank screen for most of the day. On one live board that happened literally: 8 of 19 games had four opinions and 11 had none.

The lazy fix is to fill in the missing information and price anyway. That manufactures opinions the model does not actually have, and we retired it.

What we built instead: each analyst is a **separate model at each point in the day**, trained on exactly the information that genuinely exists at that moment. When something is missing for the whole day — like a lineup — that is measured, not assumed. Across 17,926 rows, the lineup flag is 0.0% at 24, 12 and 6 hours out and 99.7% at 3 and 1 hours out. So NOVA is not merely *missing* its lineup factors early. It was never trained on them, and it cannot reach for a card nobody has posted.

When something is missing for one specific game — an unannounced starter, a plate umpire assigned late — that factor is set to neutral, contributes exactly zero, and the read publishes how complete it was.

Result: every analyst files on every game at every point in the day, 236 slots out of 236, and a fully informed read comes out bit-for-bit identical to what the engine produced before any of this existed.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### Two different kinds of "we don't know yet"

These were being confused, and separating them is the whole design.

**The information doesn't exist yet for anybody.** There is exactly one case of this, and we measured it rather than assuming it. Across 17,926 rows since January 2025, the posted-lineup flag reads **0.0000 at 24, 12 and 6 hours out, and 0.9974 at 3 and 1 hours out.** A test re-measures that against the actual data on every run, so the claim cannot drift away from reality.

A separate study confirms the same thing from the other direction. Across 568 timestamped lineups, the median posts **183 minutes** before first pitch, and clubs differ by about two hours — Pittsburgh averages 124 minutes, the Dodgers 242. Both teams have posted for **0.0%** of games at 6 hours out, **34.9%** at 3 hours, and **97.9%** at 1 hour.

**The information exists but not for this game.** MLB leaves some starters unannounced. The plate umpire is assigned late. This is checked on the actual game being priced, never decreed in advance.

### One model per analyst, per moment

| | reads | what it has 24 hours out | what fills in later |
|---|---|---|---|
| **VEGA** | the price | everything — the number exists the moment a book hangs it, and it *moves* through the day | never blocked |
| **SCOUT** | the arms | both starters once MLB names them, plus both bullpens at every point | announced starters, game by game |
| **ATLAS** | the conditions | park, altitude, roof, day or night — all fixed by the schedule days ahead | the plate umpire, late |
| **NOVA** | the bats | the *projected* card and how the two offences have been scoring | the posted lineup, at 3 hours out |

NOVA reads five factors early and seven from three hours out.

The check that proves this is one engine rather than five different ones wearing the same names: the 3-hour model reproduces the shipped 3-hour read to **exactly zero difference**.

### "Contributes nothing" needed two halves, not one

This is a small piece of arithmetic that is easy to get wrong, and getting it wrong would have been invisible.

Each analyst's signal is *its own read, minus an average*. So what a factor contributes is not just its value — it is its value *relative to the average value of that factor*.

Set a missing factor to neutral and you zero out the first half exactly. But the second half — the average — is still sitting inside the subtraction. A missing umpire would therefore push ATLAS toward the side *opposite* the average umpire. That is a real, signed contribution, made by information the analyst does not have.

So the fix removes both halves: the signal is now the sum over **only the factors actually read**. When everything is read, the correction is exactly zero and nothing changes.

### Four locks that stop this being fake coverage in a new coat

**A factor that wasn't read can't be quoted.** A neutral-filled factor contributes about zero runs but would still show up in a sorted list of drivers as something the card could cite. It gets stripped before anything can render it.

**The prose is gated on the same stamp.** Every sentence template declares what kinds of information it claims to have read. NOVA cannot say "the nine names posted tonight" on a read whose stamp says lineups were not up. ATLAS cannot mention the man behind the plate before there is one. A later refinement made this per-*factor* rather than per-*category*: ATLAS may not say "park, altitude, roof" on a read whose park row never landed, even though its venue category is technically present through day/night. A test checks both directions.

**Confidence scales with information.** A thin desk automatically produces a visibly less convinced call, with no extra machinery.

**The read says what it had.** Every read publishes its completeness, which factors were neutral-filled, and what it would have said with full information.

### One trap worth naming

Our fact table is snapshotted at each point in the day, but the enriched stats layer is joined fresh. So a card priced at midnight for 24-hours-out could otherwise read an umpire assignment that landed at noon — information from eight hours *after* the moment it claims to represent.

Every row now records whether each piece of information was actually available at that moment, and a late-arriving category that cannot be verified from the snapshot itself is **refused** rather than assumed. ATLAS reads the venue alone and says so.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
**Coverage across 97 games.** The denominator is the whole board, so a moment our collector never captured counts against us. A 24-hour-out row exists for only 69% of games; 12, 6 and 3 hours exist for 100%.

| | 24h | 12h | 6h | 3h | 1h | any point |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| VEGA | 69% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 93% | **100%** |
| ATLAS | 66% | 96% | 96% | 100% | 90% | **100%** |
| NOVA | 69% | 100% | 100% | 100% | 93% | **100%** |
| SCOUT | 62% | 90% | 90% | 100% | 92% | **100%** |

Restricted to games where a row exists at all: VEGA and NOVA are at 100% everywhere, ATLAS at 96% early (missing park rows) and SCOUT at 90% early (unannounced starters), both at 100% by three hours out. **Coverage fills in as the day progresses, which is the honest shape.**

**Everybody files.** On a recent slate, **236 of 236** analyst-and-timing slots produced a side. The old evidence floor would have silenced three of them. ATLAS runs at 70–85% completeness because the plate umpire arrives late — which is now visible on the read instead of deleting it.

**Nothing already published moved.** A fully informed read is bit-for-bit what the engine produced before any of this existed: on a settled slate, **45 of 45** complete reads reprice identically, and only reads with genuinely missing factors changed.

**Including the awkward part.** A read, once written, is frozen forever. A *stated refusal* was never an opinion and was never graded, so a slot the old rule left empty could be filled with a real read — but only once, only one-way, and only from the day the change shipped. The **126 slots the old rule left empty in July stay empty on purpose**, because the record published over those dates was computed on that population and filling them would move a published number. That count is locked by a test.

**Mixed cards are refused a pattern lookup.** Our measured desk-agreement table was built entirely on 3-hour reads, so a card whose four seats come from *different* points in the day cannot use it.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
Three ideas here travel well beyond baseball.

**Train the model for the moment it will be used in.** Fitting one 3-hour model and then feeding it imputed lineups at 24 hours out means its weights were estimated under conditions that do not exist when you actually use it. One model per moment makes the training match the deployment.

**Not knowing something has a direction.** This is the subtle one. Filling a missing value with the training average silently converts "I don't know" into "I know it's average" — which, in a model that works off deviations, is a real signed push in one direction. Without the second half of that fix, the desk would have been quietly leaning against the average umpire every single time an umpire was assigned late. Two lines of code, and it took a piece of algebra to notice.

**Both instincts about empty cards are right.** *Never show an opinion you don't have* and *never show an empty chair* are both correct, and the answer is not to pick one. It is: file on what you have, publish how much that was, scale the confidence to it, and forbid the prose from claiming anything you did not read.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
Open a game card at nine in the morning and the desk already has a view. Open it again at three in the afternoon and it has been re-read by models built for exactly that moment, with a timeline showing what each analyst said at every point along the way.

When ATLAS is running at 85% because the plate umpire has not been assigned, the card tells you, ATLAS's conviction is dialled down automatically, and ATLAS's sentence will not mention the man behind the plate.

That is the difference between a desk that always has something to say and a desk that always *sounds* equally sure — and it is what the rest of the site's honesty sits on.

---

papers.title: Yes, There's AI In Here. No, It Doesn't Pick Your Games.
papers.subtitle: We run current-generation AI across the research floor — and we locked it out of the picks by design. Then we tested it as a handicapper and published that it lost.
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
Every product says it's powered by AI. Almost none of them will tell you what that means, and none of them will show you the test.

Here is ours. DiamondEdge runs current-generation AI in three real places: models that retrain themselves every night, an AI session per analyst that writes a short note about its own slice, and multi-agent AI pipelines that mine our own accumulated failures for research ideas nobody had thought of.

What AI never does is pick a side, set a probability, move a stake, or touch a record. That is not a promise about our intentions. The pick is written and locked *before* any AI session runs, and we test it adversarially: an AI reply that tries to set the pick side, the probability, the star rating, the bet flag and the result leaves the served board **byte-for-byte identical**.

We also did the obvious experiment. We gave a frozen AI model a good pregame stat sheet and asked it to handicap totals. It lost, and not narrowly — 0.26293 forecast error against the market's 0.24890 on the same 396 games — and blending it 50/50 with the market made the market worse. Its point estimate of total runs was nearly as good as the line's. Its read on which side of the number to take was worse than saying "the base rate" every game. And it was most wrong when it was most confident.

That is why the AI in DiamondEdge sits where it sits.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### 1. Nightly retraining — the boring one that matters most

The base layer is not a language model at all. It is a training rule: to predict a given day, train only on games that had already finished before it.

That same engine produces tonight's read and rebuilds the historical replay. Behind one replay panel sit **5,894 separately trained models**. The analysts retrain monthly during evaluation and refit nightly in service. Nothing is ever scored on a game it was allowed to study, and the check that enforces that stops the program rather than logging a warning.

This is what makes "self-improving" a description rather than a slogan. The system's parameters move every night on new graded evidence, and the record it shows you is the record that discipline produced.

### 2. AI analyst notes — colour, never a call

One AI session per analyst per slate, scoped to that analyst's own stats, its own reads, and its own record.

**The entire output is two fields:** a short note, and a stance of *agree* or *careful*. There is no field for a side, a probability, a line, a stake or a star, so a session physically cannot express one.

Five separate locks, each one enough on its own:

**The pick is already decided.** Pricing fields are written once and locked *before* any session runs. The apply step copies the row forward and can only ever add advisory text. A hostile reply setting every bet-shaped field leaves the board byte-identical — and that is a test, not a hope.

**Every number has to be real.** Any number the AI writes in a note must be derivable from that game's own read row or from that analyst's own published weights. Otherwise the note is rejected.

**It can only talk about its own slice.** A note may only cite factors inside that analyst's channel.

**It can't impersonate anyone.** The prompt and the reply are both scanned for the other analysts' names and rejected if found.

**"Careful" only ever downgrades**, and grading is written from the untouched row, so a session cannot move a record in either direction.

The rule underneath all five: **AI output is treated as data, never as instructions.** A reply is parsed as JSON and its fields used as text. Nothing in a reply is executed, and nothing in a reply chooses a code path.

On the research farm the same design adds a sixth lock — **no campaigning.** A prospect's session may not claim it is winning, leading or ready for promotion, and may not reach for a betting instruction.

### 3. Multi-agent idea generation

Two pipelines, both real, both documented as experiments rather than asserted as capability.

**The archaeologist** hands our own failures to a panel. Roughly seventy closed dead ends, distilled into a ledger, plus an inventory of what data we have on disk, went to **twelve independent AI sessions, each forced through a different expert lens**: bookmaking operations, behavioural economics, atmospheric physics, scheduling, information diffusion, officiating, physiology, retail betting microstructure, media attention, panel statistics, the game theory of betting limits, and a deliberate contrarian.

The prompts contained **zero game results and zero prices**. Output was de-duplicated, scored against a rubric, and the top-ranked idea was then run as an ordinary pre-registered statistical test.

**The lab** runs four sessions in parallel, each seeing only its own analyst's performance table and available dials, each proposing changes as plain text. Every proposal gets its test written down at the moment it is queued. The lab never edits a live file — 149 serving files were hashed before and after a run with nothing changed.

### 4. The direct test

We gave a frozen AI model — one whose training ended before the season in question, so it could not have memorised results — hash-verified pregame packets: starter strikeout rate and expected damage against, team runs per game and recent form, park factor, umpire tendency, day or night. Then we asked it for the probability the total goes over the posted number, and graded it against the sharp closing price.

All 459 prompt files matched a cryptographic manifest with zero mismatches, so nobody can claim we quietly changed the question.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
### The handicapping test: a clean, significant loss

| forecaster, on the same 396 games | forecast error (lower is better) |
|---|---|
| frozen AI on a verified stat packet | **0.26293** |
| the sharp closing number | 0.24890 |
| 50/50 AI + market blend | 0.25409 |
| just say 50/50 every game | 0.25000 |
| just say the base rate every game | 0.24857 |

The AI is worse than the market by a margin the statistics say is real. It is worse than a coin flip. It is worse than a constant. And mixing it into the market made the market worse.

The diagnostics are more interesting than the headline.

**It picked under on 80.3% of games**, against the market's 44.1%. It agreed with the market's side on only 47.7% of games.

**Its confidence was backwards.** Sorted into thirds by how sure it said it was, its error rose from 0.2575 to 0.2615 to **0.2784**. It was most wrong when it was most sure — the single most dangerous property a forecaster can have.

**But it knew roughly how many runs would score.** Its average miss on the total was 3.790 runs, against the closing line's 3.734. That is genuinely impressive general knowledge. It simply had no idea which side of a sharp number that landed on.

That gap is the whole lesson. The market's advantage over a coin flip on this bet is tiny — on the order of a third of a thousandth in forecast error. Competing at that resolution requires calibration, not knowledge. Broad knowledge is not calibration.

### The idea pipeline: cheap, productive, and correctly killed

Twelve sessions produced 61 proposals, grouped to 26 mechanisms, 10 dropped, leaving **16 ranked, testable survivors**. Total cost: about 30 minutes and no marginal spend.

The top-ranked idea — a "compressed spring" effect where a total's price builds up pressure before the number itself moves — was then tested properly against 4.85 million cross-book quotes across 7,136 games.

It **passed the statistical screen**, decisively: the effect measured +0.145 runs with a range of +0.060 to +0.243 and odds against chance of less than 1 in 2,000. It survived deleting its best day. It showed up in each of three seasons separately. Of the trigger events, 23.8% saw the line move *with* the pressure and 0% moved against it.

Then it **failed on money**, also decisively: **−1.29 percentage points** of return, with a range of −2.23 to −0.55. Broken down, the line movement is worth +0.84 points and the price you pay for it costs −2.12.

The compressed spring is real. The book charges more for the spring than the release is worth.

### The lab: four candidates, zero adopted

The most recent lab run evaluated four candidates across 33,158 graded analyst rows spanning four and a half seasons. All four were **rejected**, with ranges that all contain zero.

The lab also declares its own biggest limitation in its own report rather than in a footnote: its evidence overlaps date windows that were supposed to be sealed — between 22% and 56% depending on the analyst — and therefore **lab candidates are idea generators only and can never count as confirmation**. Sealing those dates was considered and rejected on measured grounds: it would drop 55% of the history and leave a sample so thin that the error bar would be wider than the claim.

### The analyst notes, in production

First live run: 32 replies, 31 accepted, **1 rejected** for quoting a factor contribution the game's read row does not carry. That is the number validator doing exactly its job.

The run also surfaced two genuine engineering bugs — a validator that rejected an analyst quoting its own weight to four decimals, and a race condition where four parallel sessions could overwrite each other. Both fixed, both now covered by tests.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
There is a straightforward reason to be this specific.

"Powered by AI" is a claim anyone can make and nobody can check. "A hostile AI reply leaves the board byte-identical, and here is the test that proves it" is a claim that is either true or false about a running system.

The handicapping result deserves to be read carefully rather than as a punchline. A general-purpose AI, handed a good stat sheet, estimated total runs within 0.06 of a liquid betting market's closing line. That is remarkable. It was still a significant loser against that line, because the skill required is not knowing baseball — it is being calibrated to a thousandth of a percent. Publishing that null is more useful to you than any amount of AI branding.

Two things worth passing on to anyone building similar systems.

**Treat AI output as data, never as instructions.** Every lock in this architecture follows from that one sentence. Parse the reply, use its fields as text, never execute anything in it, never let it choose a code path. And the ordering — price first, *then* advise — is what turns that principle into something you can test instead of something you can forget.

**Infrastructure failures are logistics, not science, and have to be labelled that way.** Two of our four AI studies were degraded by the same boring cause: an expired credential returning an authentication error in background jobs. The handicapping study completed anyway through a different route with cryptographically identical prompts, and the change is declared in the report. The idea pipeline swapped tools, and wrote that down before generating anything. The lab strategist returned zero proposals and the report says so. None of them were quietly re-run into a cleaner-looking result.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
Every night, the models retrain on everything graded so far, about 2,848 candidate strategies get re-scored on their recent record, and the ensemble that plays tomorrow is chosen from that. That loop runs without a human in it. That is the sense in which the desk improves itself.

Alongside it, AI sessions read each analyst's slice and write a short note with an *agree* or *careful* stance. Colour, not a call.

And behind the scenes, multi-agent pipelines keep mining our own dead ends for mechanisms nobody had proposed — which is how the list of properly closed questions keeps growing.

What no AI ever does is decide your side, set your number, move your stake, or edit your record. That is a property of the code, checked every run.

papers.title: No Rewinding the Tape: Why Every Pick Was Made Before the Games Were Played
papers.subtitle: The single most common way a betting record lies is that the model got to peek. Here is the one rule that stops it, what it costs, and what it takes away from us.
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
The most common way a published betting record lies is not fraud. It is that the model got to peek.

It happens by accident and it happens constantly: a model gets tuned on the whole season and then scored on the same season; a calibration step sees the outcomes it is calibrating; a feature gets built using information that arrived after the bet would have been placed. The resulting record looks great and means nothing.

DiamondEdge has one rule that removes the entire category: **to predict a day, train only on games that had already finished before it.** One implementation, used both to build the history and to serve tonight — there is no separate "backtest mode."

This is expensive. Building one honest replay panel took 5,894 separately trained models.

It is also brutal. Ninety-eight strategies passed every check on the data we found them on, averaging 59.95%. Under this rule, on nights they had not seen, they averaged **−32.3%** and not one stayed positive. That is not the rule failing. That is the rule working, and it is why we adopted it.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### The rule

**Predict day D by training on every graded game before day D.**

Everything follows. The window *expands* over time rather than sliding, so later predictions come from better-informed models — exactly like a real system would. Refits happen monthly in the research harnesses and nightly in service.

And "train-only" means everything, not just the model. The trimming bounds, the gap-filling values, the scaling, the model weights, the calibration curve, the confidence thresholds — all of it is fitted inside the window. Nothing is fit on, or informed by, the games being scored.

There is also a declared warm-up: a minimum amount of history before a prediction counts at all, set in advance. In one study that took 9,168 eligible games down to 8,412 scored games across 727 nights, and we report the smaller number.

### The rails that make it real

**The check stops the program.** A check that logs a warning is a check somebody will ignore during a busy week. Ours raises an error and aborts the run — and it checks both the row ordering *and* the real calendar dates, because those can disagree.

**The strongest proof isn't a date filter — it's a retrain.** A date filter tests the code that was supposed to apply the fence, which is exactly the code you are worried about. So instead: physically chop the source data at the fence, *before any joining happens*, retrain every analyst from scratch, and require the weights to come out identical to nine decimal places. A single leaked game would move a weight far more than that.

**Future-blindness.** The same game must score identically whether the data behind it contains the rest of the season or is cut off at that game's own date.

### Grading by nights, not by picks

This one is unglamorous and it is why our error bars are wider than most.

Fifteen games on a Tuesday are not fifteen independent tests. They share the weather, the umpire pool, the market's mood that day. They win and lose together. Treat them as independent and your error bars come out far too narrow — you will find "significant" results in noise.

So every range we publish is built by **resampling whole nights**, with everything on them, thousands of times. On the research farm the rule is stated as a hard constraint: *nights are resampled, never games.*

The practical size of this matters. One study reports its honest sample as about **96 nights** against roughly 1,270 picks. Grading by picks there would make the error bar about three and a half times too tight.

### Sealed data is a budget, not a file

A holdout is only a holdout until you read it. So we track *families*, not files.

Before a sealed-season walk begins, the recipe, the settings, the quality gates and the statistical plan are all locked in a manifest. Each day's predictions are cryptographically committed **before** that day's results are scored. And when a better dataset came along and the walk needed re-running, the new pre-registration says so plainly: **the previous walk family is SPENT** and preserved in the log. Not a second look — a fresh experiment, with the cost of the first one on the record.

A separate first-five-innings walk is registered as a completely separate family with its own manifest, because the full-game family "is a SEPARATE walk and is not re-opened here." It even carries its defining rule in the registration itself: no bullpen stats, enforced in the code that builds the data.

Seals get proved by evidence, not assertion. One study's audit records that the sealed log's file timestamp was *unchanged* at the end of the work, and that zero sealed rows were read.

### Two kinds of record, and every row says which

Because one engine produces both, a reconstructed history and a live record are directly comparable — as long as each row states what it is. Ours do: every row carries a flag saying whether it was reconstructed or served live, and the record publishes the mix.

A reconstruction is honest *because of the fence* — the models never saw the window they are scored on — and dishonest the moment it is shown without saying so.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
### It detects a real effect

We planted one: a signal that is a coin flip for 60 nights and then 70% correct for the next 60. The nightly selection found it, playing strategies that read that source on 100% of the late nights against 21% of the early ones, and earning 58.2% from it. Then we shuffled the outcomes so no effect existed, and it earned 50.8% — which is nothing.

### It destroys fake ones

This is the more important demonstration.

98 strategies cleared every blocking check on the discovery window at a mean +14.4% return and 59.95% hit rate. Run forward: **−32.3%, zero positive, 94 outright contradicted.**

A second version of the same test: rank 1,074 strategies on the first half of the data, freeze the top 25, score them on the second half. **+2.6% becomes −7.7%, and 0 of 25 stay positive.**

### What survives is small, and precisely bounded

That is the point.

The nightly selection process replayed at 54.8% over 997 picks and 205 nights, +45.4 units, with a 90% range of −0.4% to +9.5%. Positive on both stretches it was not tuned on. Zero still inside the range.

The seven-model ceiling study's best arm got 51.510%, with a range of 50.5% to 52.6% — not distinguishable from betting the under every night.

One analyst channel measured a genuine, real effect on 8,644 games with nights-resampled error bars — and still landed at 52.34% against a 52.38% break-even. A measurable channel, not a profitable one.

Every one of those is a number you can actually act on, precisely because of how it was made.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
Three properties travel beyond this system.

**The backtest and the product have to be the same code.** The most common way a sports record lies is that the backtest used a fitting procedure, a data availability assumption, or a price convention the live system does not have. Making one function the single entry point for both removes the whole class of failure at once.

**Checks must abort, not warn.** The tournament protocol puts it in one line: a single purity violation aborts the campaign. A warning gets skipped.

**A holdout is a budget.** Tracking spent families rather than untouched files is what stops the slow leak where a "sealed" season gets peeked at four times under four different names. The most expensive example in our files is the cross-book divergence work: a sealed six-week window was **never opened at any of four consecutive stops**, and when we retired that whole idea, the only agreed route to opening it closed with it. That data is now permanently out of reach for that question. That is what a seal costs, and it is exactly what makes it worth anything.

There is a fourth point that is cultural rather than technical. This rule is unpleasant to adopt, because the very first thing it does is take away results you already believed. Ninety-eight strategies at 59.95% is a genuinely exciting screen. Watching all ninety-eight die is the moment the method proves it was worth having.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
Every record on this site was produced by a model that could have existed on the morning of the game. Not a model tuned on the season and then scored on it. Not a confidence number calibrated against results it had already seen.

That is why a DiamondEdge hit rate can be compared to a break-even number at all — and why the comparison means something.

It is also, honestly, why our numbers are smaller than the ones you will see elsewhere. A 54.8% record with a range that still touches zero is a far more honest object than a 60% backtest, and we have published exactly what happens to 60% backtests when you stop letting them rewind the tape.

---
