papers.title: Test 41 Ideas and Two Will Look Brilliant By Pure Luck. We Run the Math That Catches Them.
papers.subtitle: Write down what you're testing before you look. Count every test you ran, including the ones you threw away. And decide in advance what a boring result will mean, so you can't talk yourself out of it later.
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
Test forty-one ideas and a couple will look brilliant by pure luck. That is not a flaw in the ideas. It is arithmetic, and it is the single biggest reason most published betting edges are not real.

We handle it two ways.

**Write down what you're testing before you look.** Not just the hypothesis — the exact list of things you'll try, the settings, the rule for what counts as a pick, and the reading you'll give a boring result. That last part is the one everybody skips, and it does the most work.

**Count every test you ran.** Including the ones you threw away. Including the ones with too small a sample. A search you can shrink after the fact is not a search you can trust.

The effect of all this is entirely one-directional: it removes findings. Of 26 pre-declared ways of slicing our accuracy study, **zero survived**, with the best falling short by a factor of fourteen. Of 150 candidates in an entire analyst re-architecture, **zero passed** — and the one that cleared every accuracy gate was then disqualified for measuring nothing but the market's own price re-expressed. Of 41 desk-agreement patterns rendered on the product, **none survives**, so the insight panel ships empty.

And here is the demonstration that makes it concrete: feed the old rule a fixture of 1,200 **completely random games** and it printed three confident findings. The new rule prints zero.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### What "write it down first" actually has to fix

One file per experiment, committed before the experiment reads any data. To be worth anything, it has to nail down six things.

**The full list of what you're trying.** Our accuracy study declared seven models, A1 through A7, fully specified in advance, with the rule stated plainly: *no arm may be added, dropped, or re-specified after the fact.* A later study goes one better and states the honest version: **adding a variant after seeing results is permitted; hiding one is not.** The denominator just absorbs it.

**Every setting.** The training window, the refit schedule, the minimum sample, the trimming percentages, the gap-filling method, the model settings, the random seeds — all named up front. In our accuracy study they were explicitly copied from existing production code and **not tuned for this test**, and the stat lists were taken word-for-word from an earlier frozen report rather than re-picked.

**The pick rule.** Over if the probability is above 50%. Ties go under and still count. *There is no sitting out in the all-games number.*

**How the maths will work.** Nights resampled rather than picks, how many resamples, which seed, what kind of range, and the luck-filter plan with the exact number of tests stated.

**A hard baseline, not a coin flip.** This is the one most people get wrong. Our accuracy study's bar was not "beat 50%." It was **beat whichever constant did better — always over, or always under — with the constant allowed its best side after the fact.** The reason is in the report and the results confirmed it: *the more one-sided a model is, the better it looks, and the one-sidedness is doing the work.* A model that "hits 54%" by riding a directional bias in the sample has not demonstrated accuracy.

**What a boring result will mean.** Written down before any number exists. Our accuracy study fixed in advance that a flat confidence curve would mean *our confidence is not informative* — and it closed the escape hatch explicitly: *there is no third reading in which a single lucky bump gets promoted.*

### Counting the tests honestly

Three rules decide whether a luck filter means anything at all.

**Thin cells still count.** A split with too few games is reported as "insufficient" and **still counts in the total number of tests**. Dropping small cells after you've seen them is exactly the trick this rule exists to block.

**Pruned candidates still count.** The tournament runs its correction across every candidate ever scored, *including ones eliminated in earlier rounds*. You do not get to shrink a search by throwing away the tests that failed.

**Sweeping a threshold is not tuning — it is a search.** Stated in one line in the protocol: *a grid sweep over a threshold is not a tuning step, it is a multiple comparison.*

The research farm enforces the same logic in code rather than in prose. Its correction runs across all fourteen candidates — ten prospects plus the four incumbents, because a prospect is competing for a seat an incumbent currently holds — and the function **errors out on a family of any other size**, so nobody can quietly shrink the denominator.

### The four gates a p-value can't cover

Statistics catches one failure mode. Four more gates catch the others, and all of them block.

**Anti-trivial.** A candidate has to beat a matched always-over and always-under, has to beat **the market's own forecast accuracy**, and cannot be more than 80% one-sided.

**Throw away your best bet.** Delete the single most profitable pick. The result must still hold.

**Throw away your best night.** Delete the single best slate. Return must still be positive.

**A sample floor with a reason attached.** The maths is written into the protocol: at 200 picks across 60 nights the honest range on profit is about ±5.7 points of hit rate, and below about 30 nights the resampling method starts under-covering. Hence 200 picks over 60 nights on discovery, 60 over 20 on confirmation.

### Two cases of making an argument falsifiable instead of endless

**"It feels like it's predicting backwards."** Rather than debate that, it was registered: population fixed to one graded pick per game from a named date, null hypothesis 50%, trigger at the first moment the record hits 150 decided picks, exact interval, and a verdict of "anomaly" only if the whole range sits below 50%. The sample size was justified in advance and — critically — **fixed before the record had accrued past about 110.** Peeking is allowed descriptively; there is no verdict before the declared number.

**"Three analysts might be systematically backwards."** A bigger claim, and a sealed test was written for it. It opens with the sentence that makes the whole exercise necessary: **inverting a 43.2% sample yields 56.8% on that same sample by arithmetic, not by discovery.** So the month that produced the observation was declared inadmissible as evidence about it, a fresh 58-day window was opened, the sample size was adjusted for the fact that the three analysts' results are correlated with each other, and three kill conditions were fixed in advance — any one of which ends the hypothesis. An early stop is permitted at 400 picks because it **can only ever kill the idea, never confirm it.**

Both carry the same standing rule: **a flag does not authorise a bet.** Betting the fade would be a brand new strategy needing its own registration, its own window, its own forward evidence and its own economic gates before a single such pick is served.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
### The accuracy study's 26 splits

> Splits declared: 26. Splits tested: 26. Splits that survived: 0.

The best-looking one — favourite size between 5% and 12%, hitting 52.78% on 3,401 games — needed to clear a bar of 0.00385 and came in at 0.0555. **Short by a factor of fourteen.**

The flashiest one, June games at 53.59%, is published **uncorrected, on purpose**, so it is on the record as mined and rejected rather than quietly binned.

### The confidence question

Does the model know when it knows? Four cut-points were declared. The best model's accuracy across them ran 51.5% → 52.2% → 52.3% → 50.3% → 51.6%. Flat and non-monotone. Pre-declared reading: **our confidence is not informative.**

One model *did* produce a perfectly clean rising curve, up to 55.7% on its most confident 5%. It was not promoted, and the pre-registration is why: pooling all three models' curves as required, the strongest result anywhere came in at 0.124 against a bar of 0.00833. And the killer context — on those exact same most-confident games, **the market's own side hit 60.2%**. The model was 4.6 points *behind a free baseline* on the games it felt surest about.

### An entire re-architecture, refused

150 candidate evaluations logged across 10 runs. **Zero passed the four gates.**

One did clear all four — a price-channel variant, statistically solid on every measure. Then the pre-written anti-trivial check took it apart and found that the de-vigged market probability **on its own** scored *better* than the full channel, while the channel's actual thesis was null to slightly negative. The entire effect was the market's own number, wearing a costume.

### The insight panel

Before the filter, the product's pattern engine picked the most extreme desk-agreement cell and rendered it as a finding. Over roughly thirty near-coin-flip cells, that rule is a **finding generator**: the most extreme cell is extreme by construction.

It now computes an exact result for every row and runs one correction across all 41. Today none survives, so the panel ships **empty**.

The persuasive part is the control. We built a fixture of **1,200 purely random games**, where the most extreme cell sits 11.8 points off a coin flip. The old rule printed three findings on it. The new rule prints zero.

### The farm leaderboard

Ten prospect models, one month of results. The leader sits at 56.0% with a range that excludes a coin flip. Another sits at 44.0% with a range that *also* excludes it, in the opposite direction.

**Two of ten outside 50% is precisely what ten coin flips look like.** Which is exactly why the promotion function has no parameter that could receive a ranking, and why a test fixture leading the board at 60.4% is asserted unpromotable.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
The most useful thing about writing it down first is not that it stops fraud. It is that it stops the honest, gradual, entirely well-intentioned drift by which someone who has already seen the data picks the analysis that makes the data look meaningful.

Every step in that drift is defensible on its own. Dropping a thin cell. Adding a promising variant. Reporting the model that worked. Reading a bump as a trend. Fixing all of it in advance is the only defence, because from the inside, the drift is invisible.

Three refinements worth stealing.

**Declare the reading, not just the test.** "If the curve is flat, our confidence is not informative" is a stronger commitment than any threshold, because it removes the wiggle room that survives a p-value.

**Make the bar the hard baseline, not zero.** Beating a coin flip is irrelevant when a free constant beats a coin flip. Beat the constant.

**Add an anti-trivial breakdown to every gate.** Our re-architecture is the cleanest case: a candidate passed a significance test, a forecast-accuracy test and a luck filter, and was still measuring nothing but the market's own number. Rediscovering that a sharp market is well-priced is the market working, not a finding.

One last note, from the accuracy study, about why this kind of null is worth so much. Under this protocol, a null is the result *least* likely to be overturned by better data — because the failure is not "we lacked information." One of our models had 98 different stats and scored 50.131%, essentially a coin flip.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
You will notice that the desk's insight panel is often empty. That is the filter running.

The rule that used to fill it — show the most extreme pattern — is a finding generator when every pattern is near a coin flip. It has been replaced by a rule that requires a pattern to survive being checked against all 41 before it can be said out loud. Every line that does render now carries its sample size, its exact range, and the words "not distinguishable from a coin flip" when the range crosses 50%.

The same discipline is why this site does not advertise a 60% strategy. Strategies at 60% show up in every single search we run. None of them have survived being counted properly. What is left is what did.

papers.title: The Prices We Were Betting Into Did Not Exist
papers.subtitle: For a while, 34 of our 58 live picks were graded against prices no bettor could have taken. A wrong price doesn't just mis-grade a bet — it CHOOSES the bet. Here are four separate bugs, and the one rule that ended them.
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
The most dangerous bug in a betting system is not a wrong final score. It is a wrong **price** — because the price is exactly what decides whether something becomes a bet. A fake price does not merely mis-grade a pick. It *manufactures the edge that selected it.*

We found four of these, independently, over about three days. The worst one meant **34 of our 58 live served picks were priced above the best real quote at their own number.** Re-priced honestly, the average claimed edge on those picks fell from +5.29% to +1.65%, and only 29 of the 58 still cleared the bar.

The fix is one sentence, enforced in one place, imported everywhere:

> A served price must come from **one coherent market** and be simultaneously **at the pick's own number**, from the **full-game market**, and **live at the moment we decided** — from a book actually posting right then. Fail any clause and the row is **unpriceable**, not priced off the next best thing.

The cost of that rule turned out to be almost nothing: 99.36% of games still carry a real book on the consensus total. It removes fictional coverage, not real coverage.

And we did not go back and fix the record. History is not repaired and not re-priced. The four bugs are published with exact counts, and the one served pick that sat on a corrupted line is named.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### Bug 1 — the price was for a different total

Our "best price" column was built as the best price across all books **at each book's own posted total**, with no filter. So a pick on 8.5 could be paid at a price quoted on 9.0.

The report puts the consequence precisely: *the row was graded at the pick's number but paid at another number's price — a price no bettor could take — and because that price is exactly what the bet-or-pass gate evaluates, it manufactured the edge that selected the pick.*

Measured on live picks: **34 of 58** were priced above the best real quote at their own number, by an average of 0.077 in decimal odds. Re-gate honestly and 29 of 58 survive; the average claimed edge drops from **+5.29% to +1.65%**.

### Bug 2 — the price came from a different market

The snapshot read was not capped at first pitch, so in-play "runs remaining" quotes could leak into a pregame full-game decision. Fixed by capping the read at first pitch.

### Bug 3 — the book had already gone home

Our snapshot logic took each book's *last* quote at or before the decision moment. That carries forward the final quote of a book that stopped posting hours earlier, and lets it win the best-price contest.

Caught on one game: a 24-hours-out row priced UNDER 9.0 at −107 from a book whose last quote was **1 hour 44 minutes earlier**. At the moment we decided, that book was not in the market at all, and the best real UNDER 9.0 was −110.

**We measured the tolerance rather than picking one.** Across 22,562 checks in a single month, 96.6% of books are present in the snapshot itself — and **nothing at all sits between 0 and 5 minutes of staleness.** The collector runs every 10 minutes, so a book is either in this snapshot or a full cycle behind. There is no middle ground to be lenient about.

And a book that misses a cycle usually never comes back: **78–92% absent** at 5–15 minutes, **81–86%** past two hours, against just **1.6%** for books present in the snapshot. When one does return, it brings the identical number and price only 0–53% of the time, against 88.7% for books that were there all along.

Tolerance set at **2.0 minutes**, from that distribution.

Blast radius: **77 of 3,492 price cells over a month (2.21%)** were won by a departed book, faking a payout 2.38% richer on average — median 1.49%, maximum **48.6%**.

Two more cells had *only* a carried-forward quote and became honestly unpriceable.

### Bug 0 — two different ballgames under one ID

Quote rows for two different games were stored under a single game identifier: **580 affected snapshots since 2026-07-18**, across four games.

The mechanism needed two things to go wrong at once. All four were game two of a split doubleheader whose game one was a rainout makeup, so the schedule carried a stale "Postponed" listing that won a de-duplication tiebreak and shifted the record by about eighteen hours. And our event matcher had a six-hour tolerance that could match many events to one game. Every foreign event sat **5 hours 29 minutes to 5 hours 59 minutes** from its host — the thirty-one-minute band immediately under the old tolerance.

Blast radius, exact: **14 consensus cells moved**, the worst being a total served at 12.5 whose true value was 9.0, plus several spread cells that flipped sign. Nineteen underlying rows were touched (1.27% of 1,501). **Exactly one served pick** sat on a corrupted line, and it graded a loss.

**The near miss is the part that should worry you.** One row carried a pick on UNDER 12.5, flagged as a take, tiered Strong, at +140 — and graded a **win** at 12.5. That game's actual market ran 8.5 to 9.5 at 23 books all day. The 12.5 came from the *other* game's books quoting in play. It reached the payload as a pass only because an unrelated evidence check happened to demote it.

> Nothing in the pipeline knew the line was fictional.

The fix resolves one event per game or refuses outright. And the window was chosen from a measurement rather than a guess: 94.1% of event-to-game pairs sit within 30 minutes — but the separation is not clean. Four legitimate games sit at 222 to 299 minutes out, and one of the corrupted events sat 179 minutes *inside*. When the two populations overlap, refusing is the only correct answer.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
**The rule barely costs coverage.** After enforcement, **1,695 of 1,706 (99.36%)** of game-and-moment cells still carry at least one real book on the consensus total.

**It is enforced by automated checks, not by review.** A scan runs every intraday cycle and publishes its result whether or not it fires. A serving self-test carries the check together with a **deliberate failing control**, so a check that would pass on anything gets caught. Three failure codes get emitted: *wrong number*, *wrong market*, *stale quote*.

**It propagates upstream into research.** The strategy tournament scores at flat standard juice rather than reconstructed prices, and says why: reconstructing a price would not satisfy this rule, and quoting the best-price column is exactly the defect that inflated 34 of 58 served picks.

**The gate downstream of it is what turns a price into a decision.** Being on the right side of the line is never sufficient. Simulating a small model edge across every real market and price, **938 of 1,152 "correct side" candidates flip to no-bet — 81.4%**, rising to 97.4% on moneylines. Price coverage is complete: 553 of 553 replay rows and 132 of 132 live rows carry a real per-side price, with no fallback anywhere.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
**A price bug is a selection bug.** This is why price validity is a research-integrity issue rather than an accounting one. A wrong score mis-grades a pick you already made. A wrong price *chooses the pick*. All four of these bugs had the same signature, and in three of the four the bug made us look **better** than we were.

**Set tolerances from data, not from instinct.** A five-minute staleness tolerance would have sounded eminently sensible — and would have been exactly wrong, because there is nothing between zero and five minutes in the actual distribution. The two-minute number is a reading of the data, not a judgement call.

**Refuse on ambiguity rather than resolving it plausibly.** The fourth bug's fix could have simply taken the nearest event. 94.1% of pairs are within half an hour, so that would have looked fine. It would also have silently mis-assigned four legitimate games and one corrupted one. When two populations overlap, refusing costs one row and a plausible guess costs an unknown number of them.

**And history stays as it was.** Write-once is absolute. The tool that could rewrite past prices is disabled behind an explicit flag literally named `--i-am-restating-history`. The affected games are named in a published disclosure list rather than edited out. A record you are willing to rewrite when it embarrasses you is not a record.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
Every price attached to a pick here is a price that existed — at that number, in the full-game market, at that moment, from a book that was actually posting. When no such price exists, the row shows as unpriceable and cannot become a bet. It does not quietly get paid at the next best number.

It also means a pick has to clear a **price** test, not just a side test. When the desk clearly likes a game and no pick appears, that is usually this: the model likes the side and the price does not pay for it.

And when we found that all of this had not always been true, the record did not change. Four bugs are documented with exact counts, the single served pick that sat on a corrupted line is named, and the ledger it was graded in still says what it said. That is the trade: a slightly worse-looking history, and a record you can actually rely on.

papers.title: Two Sources Have To Agree On the Score Before We'll Grade Your Bet
papers.subtitle: We thought we had a second opinion on every final. It turned out our second opinion was being fed by the first one. Here's what we built instead.
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
Every record a betting product shows you rests on one boring fact per game: the final score.

Ours read finals from MLB's official API, and cross-checked them against a local database that *looked* like a second opinion. It was not. That database was being fed from the same API. Two readings of one source will always agree, and their agreement proves absolutely nothing.

So we rebuilt it. Grading now checks against a same-source copy (labelled honestly as exactly that, because it can only catch our own parsing and joining bugs), and against ESPN — genuinely different reporters, a genuinely different pipeline. The engine's own stored values were later added as a fourth check.

And the behaviour on disagreement is the important part: **the game is not graded.** Not dropped, not resolved by majority vote. It stays on the board until they agree.

We then re-checked the entire historical corpus back to March 2022: **11,026 finals, zero disagreements, zero flipped scores.** The first live month: 280 of 280.

The value of that is not the bugs it caught. It is that a clean grade now means something about the world instead of something about our own parser — and that the exact same class of failure had already been found, one layer down, in the same system.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### Why a second opinion from the same source is worth nothing

Two readings of one feed are one reading.

The distinction matters more than it sounds, because there are two genuinely different failure types.

A **single upstream feed can be wrong** about a game. Rare, but it happens, and no amount of internal cross-checking will ever see it.

Far more commonly, **our own handling is wrong**: a parsing error, a bad join, a doubleheader collapsed into one row, an ID reused across two games.

A same-source copy catches all of the second type and none of the first. So the rail uses it — and **labels it as exactly that** rather than presenting it as independence it does not have.

### The genuinely independent check

ESPN is a separate newsroom with separate reporters, separate ingestion and separate ways of being wrong. It is the axis that can catch a wrong upstream feed, and it is checked on every graded game.

The engine's own stored values were added later, giving four independent readings of the same fact before any record moves.

### Designed to fail safe, not fail open

**Disagreement blocks grading.** A game whose final disagrees is not graded, not pruned, and stays on the board. It does not get resolved by majority vote, and it does not quietly vanish from the denominator — which would be its own subtle form of record manipulation.

**A broken check degrades to grading-with-disclosure, rather than taking the whole night down.** A verification system that halts the entire pipeline because a third-party endpoint is slow will be switched off within a month. This one survives its own outage without becoming either a liar or a blocker.

**Ambiguity returns nothing.** A 45-minute guard returns no match rather than guessing when a stale start time sits exactly between two candidate games. Same principle as the price rules: a plausible guess is worse than a stated absence, because it is invisible.

### Why we stopped trusting game IDs

The specific form this rail takes exists because the identical failure was found — and measured — one layer down.

A 19.2-million-row historical odds table keyed its pregame quotes to game IDs by matching team names within a date, with no check that the quoted event was actually the game that ID names. On one verified example: **a single game ID holding 1,003 pregame rows for that game and 1,441 pregame rows for the next day's game.**

Across the archive, the share of game IDs holding more than three hours of different start times ran from **55.3% in 2021 to 67.8% in 2026** — worse over time, not better, because every row came from the same collector with the same bug.

Two consequences fed straight into how grading works now.

**The most natural way to pull a closing line is the most exposed one.** Taking the last pregame snapshot per game ID — the obvious approach — lands on the *wrong game* between 50.8% and 62.1% of the time depending on season, on average four to seven hours after the true first pitch. In the report's words: *"last pregame snapshot per game_pk" is the most exposed pattern, not a safe one.*

**And there was a date bug underneath, which had already misled a report.** Our games table stores the **UTC date of first pitch**, which agrees with MLB's official local date only **97.7%** of the time. A small, systematic 2.3% offset, invisible until measured, that quietly breaks any date-keyed join.

The fix was to build the identity layer the data never had: a map of 13,429 distinct events with all **19,192,231 rows** re-mapped, resolving 96.7% of events to a game and returning **nothing rather than a guess** on the remaining 447. The collector, the live feed — which turned out to be **61% contaminated**, 292 of 480 game IDs — and the serving path were all fixed to require start-time proximity. The production feed our shipped models actually use was audited and found already correct.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
**Live.** 280 of 280 July finals agree across sources, and all 280 are independently confirmed by the separate newsroom.

**Historical.** An offline audit of the full research corpus back to March 2022 compared **11,026 finals with zero disagreements and zero flipped scores.**

That second check deserves emphasis, because almost nobody runs it. A flipped score is home and away transposed. It leaves the **total correct**, so every totals bet still grades fine — while silently inverting every run-line and moneyline bet built on the same row. A totals check cannot see it. Zero across 11,026 games is a meaningful clean bill precisely *because* it could have failed on its own.

**Fourth axis.** Adding the engine's own stored values produced zero disagreements as well.

**Standing conclusion.** Every outcome the records rest on is now independently corroborated rather than self-consistent.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
The obvious objection is that this found nothing. Eleven thousand games, four sources, zero disagreements. So why build it?

Because the value of a verification check is not the bugs it catches. It is what it lets you claim afterward. Before, "our records agree with the source" was a statement about our parser. Now, a clean grade is a statement about the world. Those are different claims, and only the second one can support a published record.

There is also a base-rate argument. In the same period, this program found four independent price bugs and a 19.2-million-row identity contamination affecting roughly half the archive in some seasons. The belief that outcome data is somehow uniquely immune to the failures that hit every other data layer is not a belief worth holding on faith. It was worth checking, and it came back clean — which is a result, not a non-result.

Two principles generalise.

**Independence has to be architectural, not nominal.** Two readings of one feed are one reading. This rail labels its same-source copy honestly rather than counting it as a second opinion, and documents exactly which failure type each axis can and cannot catch.

**"We can't grade this yet" is a legitimate answer.** Most systems have only two states for a game: graded, or dropped. Dropping is quietly destructive — it removes a row from a denominator because of a data problem, which is a mild form of choosing your own sample. Leaving the game ungraded and visible on the board is the honest third option, and it is what we use.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
When a game gets graded here, at least two genuinely independent sources agreed on what happened, and the home and away scores were checked in the right order.

When they disagree, the game sits on the board ungraded until they agree. It does not get quietly resolved in a direction, and it does not quietly disappear.

Combined with the rule that a graded row is frozen forever, that is what makes the published record an audit trail rather than a summary. It does not get corrected in our favour later, and it is not built on a final score only one source ever saw.

papers.title: We Redid One of Our Own Predictions By Hand To Make Sure the Computer Wasn't Lying
papers.subtitle: A program that agrees with itself proves nothing. So we re-cut a training set on paper, re-solved the weights, and recomputed one probability from scratch: 0.497780783 both ways.
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
A computer program that agrees with itself proves nothing about whether it is computing the right thing.

So for our biggest study, we took one specific prediction — a June 2024 game on a total of 8.5 — and rebuilt it entirely by hand, outside the program. We re-cut that fold's training data manually (4,824 games, latest one dated 2024-05-31), re-solved the model weights from scratch, took the raw inputs and trimmed, filled and scaled them by hand, and recomputed the probability.

By hand: **0.497780783.** From the pipeline: **0.497780783.** Difference: exactly zero.

That is one of five layers. Above it sit eight automated checks that all have to pass before anyone is allowed to look at a result. Below it sit controls that are *required to fail* on random data, and a standing practice of attacking our own already-banked findings.

That last layer found the biggest thing in these files: a 19.2-million-row odds archive where, in the most affected extraction pattern, **more than a fifth of quote cells were contested between two different ballgames, and the wrong game's listing won 99.7% of the contests.** It had been quietly wrong for years.

No positive conclusion rested on it. We withdrew about fourteen of our own published nulls anyway, and explained why.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### Layer 1 — automated gates that block

Every campaign runs an audit block that must pass in full before a single result is read.

| check | what it looks for | result |
|---|---|---|
| banned words | any stat whose name contains "closing", "final", "result", the score itself | **111 stats, 0 violations** |
| timing | every decision stands before first pitch | **9,168 checked, 0 violations** |
| wall discipline | no stats from a later point in the day | **34 columns, zero from the wrong moment** |
| joins | only on the game identifier | **3 joins, all clean** |
| the seal | development data ends where it should; nothing sealed was read | **0 sealed rows; file timestamp unchanged** |
| train-only fitting | trimming, filling, scaling, weights, calibration, thresholds | **all inside the training window** |
| spend | external data calls | **0 calls, $0** |
| fold ordering | training always ends before evaluation begins | **every fold** |

Two of these are stronger than they look. The timing check does not just report "no violations" — the lead time's **minimum, median and maximum are all exactly 180.0 minutes**, which means every decision row stands precisely where it claims rather than merely somewhere before first pitch. And the seal is verified by *file evidence*: the sealed log's modification timestamp was unchanged at the end of the study, rather than someone promising nobody opened it.

### Layer 2 — prove the fence by retraining, not by filtering

The strongest available proof that a training fence held is not a date filter, because a date filter tests exactly the code you are worried about.

So instead: physically chop the source data at the fence, **before any joining happens**, retrain every analyst from scratch, and require the resulting weights to be identical to nine decimal places. A single leaked training game would move a weight far more than that.

The same technique runs a level deeper on the research farm, verified *upstream of every derived column*, alongside checks that schedule-based features cannot see the future and that the posted line does not sneak into any model that is supposed to be independent of it.

### Layer 3 — redo one prediction by hand

The one check a self-consistent program cannot pass by being self-consistent.

Take one game. Re-cut its training data by hand. Refit the scaling on it. Re-solve the weights. Take the raw inputs as they stood at the decision moment and trim, fill and scale them by hand. Recompute the probability.

| | |
|---|---|
| by hand | **0.497780783** |
| from the pipeline | **0.497780783** |
| difference | **0.0** |

The pick was UNDER; the game produced 6 runs; the prediction was right. But that is not the point. The point is that the number the program produced is the number the stated method produces.

This recurs across campaigns as a required item. A network-based study hand-recomputed a derived game statistic and got 6.245849 against a stored 6.245849. An ensemble study hand-recomputed a probability to sixteen decimal places and matched exactly. A pattern study hand-recomputed two of its statistics. An astronomy study cross-checked its sun-position engine against a completely independent implementation, agreeing to within 0.05 degrees, and hand-verified one game's shadow index.

There is a production version too: a single command prints every multiplication in an analyst's read, so any pick you see on the site can be recomputed on paper.

### Layer 4 — controls that have to fail

A check that has never fired might be a check that *cannot* fire. So several ship with a deliberate failing control.

A serving self-test carries a negative control alongside its real check. The desk's pattern engine carries a fixture of **1,200 purely random games** — where the most extreme cell sits 11.8 points off a coin flip, and the old rule printed three findings while the corrected rule prints zero. The strategy tournament validated its selection on a **planted** effect and required it to earn nothing when the outcomes were shuffled. The analyst rebuild ran a pure-noise control and a line-only control alongside its real candidates, and both came back null as required.

A structural variant of the same idea: the farm's promotion function is verified to have **no parameter that could receive a ranking**, checked by inspecting its own signature, and verified never to import the leaderboard, checked by inspecting its own source code. A test fixture leading the board at 60.4% is asserted unpromotable.

### Layer 5 — attack your own results, on a schedule

Periodically, we go after our own banked findings looking for contamination. The largest such audit is below, and it is why this is a standing practice rather than an incident response.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
### The big audit

A routine check flagged possible ID contamination in a 19.2-million-row historical odds archive that several banked results leaned on.

**Scope.** The share of game IDs holding more than three hours of different start times rose from **55.3% in 2021 to 67.8% in 2026** — worse over time, because every row came from the same collector with the same bug. Among contaminated IDs, 60–64% of pregame rows in recent seasons belong to a *different* event. Taking the last pregame snapshot per ID — the most common approach in the exposed studies — lands on the wrong game **50.8% to 62.1%** of the time, on average four to seven hours after the true first pitch.

**Exact measurement on one study family.** 2,399,304 quote cells; **533,733 contested (22.25%)**; the wrong game's listing won **532,103 of them — 99.7% of contests.**

**Root cause.** The collector matched each date's schedule on team names only, with no start-time check — so tomorrow's game, already on the board, got stamped with today's ID. A dictionary overwrite silently dropped the second game of every doubleheader. The collection window ran four hours past the last start. And a helper function *fabricated* a first-inning, no-score game state for any snapshot taken before the first play, which is why quotes for a game that had not started looked like in-play rows.

**The honest accounting, in both directions.**

> No banked positive conclusion rests on the contaminated data — every exposed study had published a null. But roughly a dozen of those nulls are unreliable as evidence, and must not be cited as constraints.

And, symmetrically:

> No positive result flipped to negative. Nothing banked or shipped sits on the affected data. Negative results flipping to positive is possible, but unknowable without re-running.

Roughly **fourteen of about seventy** banked nulls were re-flagged as not informative. They were not deleted and they were not defended. They were downgraded, in public, with the reason attached.

**The fix.** A map of 13,429 distinct events with all **19,192,231 rows** re-mapped, resolving 96.7% of events to a game and returning nothing rather than a guess on 447 ambiguous cases. The collector was fixed to require start-time proximity. The **live** feed turned out to have the same bug — 61% contaminated, 292 of 480 IDs — and was fixed. The serving path now returns a quote eight minutes before first pitch where it previously returned tomorrow's line ten hours after the game had ended. The production feed our shipped models actually use was audited and found already correct.

**And the audit corrected itself.** In the process, the auditors found that their own motivating example had been misread: the games table stores the *UTC* date of first pitch, matching MLB's official local date 97.7% of the time. The report fixes its own opening rather than quietly leaving it.

### Ordinary leaks, caught by ordinary checks

The discipline catches everyday mistakes too, which is the common case. A data build's own leak check found that the lineups spine kept the **original scheduled date for 143 postponed or rescheduled games** — a genuine timing leak, fixed and re-verified across every sampled date.

The same build spot-checked five derived numbers against the upstream source and matched exactly on all five, including a strikeout rate recomputed from raw counts (98 strikeouts in 336 batters faced) and a three-year park factor.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
**Automated gates catch the mistakes you thought of.** They are necessary, cheap, and not enough. Every gate encodes a guess about how a leak could happen, and the interesting leaks are the ones nobody guessed.

**Doing it by hand catches the ones you didn't.** It is the only check here that is genuinely independent of the program's own assumptions, because it re-derives the number from the stated method rather than from the code. It is also expensive — about one prediction per campaign is what is affordable — which is why it gets spent on the main result.

**Controls that must fail are how you know a check works.** A check that has never fired is indistinguishable from a check that cannot. The random-games fixture is the clearest case: it converts "our filter seems strict" into "our filter prints zero findings on data with zero findings in it, and the old one printed three."

**Attacking your own results has to be scheduled, not triggered.** The archive contamination existed for years, sat underneath multiple published studies, and produced no symptom — because every affected study returned a null, and a null is exactly what contaminated data produces. The audit was worth running precisely when nothing looked wrong.

That last point has a corollary about how to report it. The contamination did not overturn a single positive claim, and it would have been very easy to say that and stop. Instead we worked out which *nulls* it had made meaningless, published the count, and withdrew them — because a null we cite as a reason not to pursue something is a load-bearing claim, and a load-bearing claim built on a wrong market anchor has to come down just as a positive one would.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
The numbers on this site were produced by pipelines that have been attacked by the people who built them. Every campaign carries a block of checks that had to pass before anyone was allowed to look at a result. Every fence is proved by retraining rather than asserted by filtering. At least one prediction per major study was recomputed by hand, outside the program, and had to match to nine decimals.

And when the checks found something — a 19.2-million-row archive that had been quietly wrong for years — the response was not a silent patch. It was a published report with exact counts, a named list of what was and was not affected, about fourteen of our own previously banked results downgraded, and a correction to the audit's own opening example.

That is what the word *audit* is supposed to mean.

papers.title: Some Nights There Are Only Two Picks. We Checked Whether That's Us Being Too Strict.
papers.subtitle: A third of nights were producing two picks or fewer. So we graded every near-miss. Every relaxation was a measured loser — except one, and here's exactly how honestly we shipped it.
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
Some nights DiamondEdge shows you two picks. Some nights it shows you none. That is a fair thing to complain about, so we tested it properly rather than adjusting a dial.

Across 117 nights, **38 of them (32%) produced two picks or fewer**, and 17 produced none at all. So we took every candidate that *just missed* the price gate, graded it, and asked: were we too strict?

**No.** Every price relaxation is a measured loser or noise. The band closest to the gate graded 43.9% and −14.0%. The band furthest away graded best — which is not a gradient, it is noise, and it means loosening would have surfaced measured losers. The gate stayed, unchanged, not loosened by one basis point.

One real finding did come out of it. The *conviction* floor — how much the model has to disagree with the market — sat half a notch too high. Picks clearing the **full** price gate at conviction between 0.0075 and 0.010 graded **104-78-4: 57.1%, +15.7% return**, positive in both halves of the window and on both sides. The band just below graded −14.2%. The cut is exactly at 0.0075, and we say so rather than rounding to a nicer number.

The interesting part is how that shipped: **served record starting 0-0-0**, half stake, the 104-78-4 labelled BACKTEST everywhere it renders, graded in its own separate ledger, and no historical pick promoted into it.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### The gate

A pick requires the price to pay more than the model's edge is worth, by a declared margin. The rule, in the specification: **"right side of the line" alone is never a pick.**

The worked example makes it better than any argument. A run-line favourite at −196, with the model giving it a 64% chance, **fails** — you need 66.2% to break even at that price. The model likes the side and the price makes it a loser. Give it a 70% chance and it becomes a pick.

Every price used is a real per-side price, at all five points in the day, with no fallback anywhere.

### How much that gate actually does

This is bigger than it looks. Simulating a small model edge across every real market and price in our corpus:

| model edge | "right side" candidates | that survive the price test | that fail |
|---|---|---|---|
| **+1%** | 1,152 | **214** | **938 — 81.4%** |
| +2% | 1,152 | 846 | 306 — 26.6% |
| +3% | 1,152 | 1,145 | 7 — 0.6% |
| +5% | 1,152 | 1,152 | 0 |

By market at +1%: **moneylines lose 97.4%** of their correct-side candidates, spreads 72.9%, totals 74.0%.

The shape is the point. A small directional edge is almost entirely destroyed by price. A large one survives it. That is precisely why the gate exists — and why "we were on the right side 55% of the time" is not a claim about money.

### The pressure test

Rather than argue about coverage, we graded every near-miss on leak-safe data and asked a genuinely two-sided question: is the gate too tight, or is a thin night the honest answer?

Candidates were tallied by cause of death: 252 died on price, 223 on the conviction floor, 170 for having no conviction row at all, and 353 across three near-miss price bands.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
### The price gate must stay

Each relaxation band, graded:

| band | record | hit | return | range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| just below the gate | 50-64-3 (n=117) | **43.9%** | **−14.0%** | −32.0% to +3.9% |
| further below | 53-59-2 (n=114) | 47.3% | −6.9% | −25.2% to +11.3% |
| furthest below (control) | 58-52-3 (n=113) | 52.7% | +2.7% | −15.6% to +20.9% |

The verdict is one line: **every price relaxation band is a measured loser or noise.**

And look at the shape. The band **closest** to the gate is the worst, and the control **furthest** from it is the best. That is not a gradient — it is noise. A "just take the top few every night" rule drawing on these bands would surface measured losers. It was rejected.

A second relaxation was tested and rejected: combining moderate conviction with a sub-gate price graded 103-123-5 at −10.5%, and the combination of high conviction with a sub-gate price **literally never occurs**.

A third proposal — blending in another probability source — was rejected on coverage grounds rather than accuracy: the component it would have blended prices only about two games a night.

### The conviction floor was half a notch too high

The one real finding. Picks clearing the **full** price gate, with the model-versus-market gap in the band 0.0075 to 0.010:

**104-78-4 — 57.1% hit rate (range 49.9% to 64.1%), +15.7% return (range +1.1% to +30.3%)** — positive in both halves of the window and on both sides.

The band immediately below, 0.0050 to 0.0075, graded 47-64-4 at **−14.2%**. The cut is exactly at 0.0075.

Coverage effect over the same window, as a would-have: picks per night **4.31 → 5.94**; nights with two or fewer **39 → 17**; nights with zero **17 → 3**. It concentrates on exactly the thin nights — quiet slates with small edges — which is the shape you want from a coverage fix, and not the shape you get from just lowering the bar everywhere.

### How it shipped

This is the part that matters most, because a +15.7% backtest is exactly the kind of number that normally becomes a marketing headline.

| rail | what it does |
|---|---|
| activation date | the band is dated to the day it shipped; **no historical pick is retroactively promoted** |
| served record starts **0-0-0** | its public record begins empty and accrues live |
| the 104-78-4 is labelled **BACKTEST** everywhere | it is never shown as a served result |
| half stake | 0.5 units, regardless of how many stars it displays |
| separate ledger | graded on its own, not folded into the headline record |
| precedence | a core pick always beats an expanded one |
| frozen | anything already served is untouched |

Post-ship reconciliation confirmed nothing else moved: the headline record matched exactly, the beta stream was unchanged, and both self-test suites passed including seven new checks written for the band.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
**A directional record is not an economic record.** The flip table makes that quantitative rather than rhetorical: at a small edge, 81% of correct-side opinions are unprofitable bets, and on moneylines 97% are. Any published hit rate that does not come with the price it was available at is under-specified, which is why every number here comes with a break-even next to it.

**Grade the near-misses before you widen the gate.** The instinct when coverage is thin is to relax the threshold. The instinct is usually wrong, and here the data said so unambiguously: the relaxation bands lose, and the band nearest the gate is the worst of them. Grading them turned a product argument into a measurement.

**The conviction result is a different kind of thing, and that difference is why it was allowed.** The rejected relaxations lower the **economic** bar — they take bets whose price does not justify them. The accepted widening keeps the economic bar fully intact and lowers only the **disagreement** bar, admitting picks where the model and the market are close but the price is genuinely good. Two different dials. Only one moved.

**And the process is the point.** A 57.1% record on 104-78-4 with a range clearing zero is a good result. It is also, unavoidably, the output of a search across our own near-misses — and the honest way to treat that is as a hypothesis, not as a record.

So it shipped as one: activation-dated, at half stake, in its own ledger, with a served record starting at zero and every historical pick behind it labelled BACKTEST. If the band is real, its live record will say so in a few months. If it is not, the live record will say that instead — and the headline record will not have been contaminated either way.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
The picks you see cleared a **price** test, not just a side test. When the desk clearly likes a game and no pick appears, that is usually this: the model likes the side and the price does not pay for it.

Some nights there are two picks. That is the honest output of a slate where nothing was priced well — and this study is the evidence that filling those nights by lowering the bar would have handed you measured losers.

And where the bar did move — one measured half-notch on conviction, with the price gate untouched — the widened band's public record started at 0-0-0 on the day it shipped. Nothing was backdated into it.

papers.title: Our Analysts Thought They Were Beating the Number. They Were Betting It Back at Itself.
papers.subtitle: Three of our four analysts were supposed to have their own read on a game. It turned out the market's number already contained most of it — so their records were really a bet on which way the month's totals fell.
papers.category: What We Know About the Market
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
This is the most important thing we have found, and it is about us, not about baseball.

Three of our four analysts were designed to bet their own read of a game — the arms, the bats, the conditions — and specifically *not* the market. Each one projected a total, subtracted a rolling average, and bet the difference. The intent was that subtracting an average removes the posted number from the decision.

It does not. We measured the thing they were betting to be **51% the same as the posted total**, with the market moving its number about **1.03 runs for every run** of it. In other words, the market already contained almost exactly the quantity each analyst thought was its own contribution.

The consequence is worse than being wrong. It means their published records were partly a bet on **which way that month's totals happened to fall** — a lottery ticket, not a measurement. A 43% month and a 57% month could be the exact same model.

We rebuilt them so the signal is genuinely independent of the price. It worked: average overlap with the line fell from 0.355 to 0.033, and on the same 374 games ATLAS went from 63% mixed up with the line and hitting 44.26%, to independent and hitting 49.73%.

**Accuracy did not improve.** Zero of 150 candidates passed the four gates we wrote before starting. What we bought was not an edge. It was the ability to know what our own records mean.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### The symptom, and the tempting wrong answer

One analyst's published July record was 43.2%.

The obvious read — and it was argued for internally, seriously — is that the channel might be systematically *backwards*. If it is, inverting it is worth a lot of money.

That was refused on arithmetic grounds before it was tested, in a sentence that deserves to be on a wall somewhere:

> **Inverting a 43.2% sample yields 56.8% on that same sample by arithmetic, not by discovery.**

A sealed test was written to settle it on a *fresh* window, because the month that generated an observation cannot confirm it.

And the competing explanation is what this paper is about. The analysts are not backwards. Their side is largely a restatement of the posted number, so their hit rate simply tracks whatever the month's over/under split happened to be — around a true rate of 50%.

### The measurement

Two questions settle it.

**How much of the analyst is already in the price?** Regress the posted total on the analyst's signal: the slope is about **1.03 runs of line per run of signal**, and the overlap reaches **0.509**. Those channels are already fully inside the number.

**What's left after the market has spoken?** Regress what actually happened, relative to the line, on the analyst's signal. On the original training window that came out at +0.006 for the arms channel and −0.014 for the conditions channel — both statistically indistinguishable from zero.

The finding underneath is important and easy to misread as a contradiction: **23 of 24 declared factor directions are confirmed by the data** when each factor is asked on its own. The factors are *right about baseball*. They are simply not *news*, because the market already read them.

### Three fixes tried, one shipped

**Fit on the difference from the line instead of the total.** Over-corrects: the conditions channel swung from +0.509 overlap to −0.342. And the general lesson is worth keeping: changing what you predict does not un-mix your *inputs*. A park factor is tangled up with the posted total no matter what you regress it on.

**Strip the line out of every input before fitting.** This achieves independence — and destroys the one channel that had something. The bats channel collapsed from a real effect to nothing, with the change statistically significant *in the wrong direction*. Stripping the market out of every input also strips the channel's own information out with it.

**Fit normally, then subtract the line's influence from the finished view.** This shipped. The design principle, in one line: *the line is something to remove, not something to predict with. It carries no weight of its own — it can only ever take something away.*

A test verifies the property directly: flatten the line to a constant and the signal shifts by exactly the removal term and nothing else, to sixteen decimal places. And a gate errors out if any price column reaches a channel that is supposed to be independent of price.

### The evaluation

Written and sealed before a single number existed, and run on **11,559 graded, priced games from March 2022 to August 2026** — against the 3,748 the old version was fitted on. Every factor is at least 90% filled back to 2022, so the extra 7,811 games are real coverage rather than a data artefact.

Three windows: the pre-declared primary (3,748 games), a bigger power window (**8,644 games across 707 nights**), and a post-fence confirmation window (374 games, deliberately underpowered).

Five gates were declared in advance, including one that turned out to matter enormously: an **anti-trivial** check requiring that any effect survive having the market's own number stripped out of it.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
### The architecture claim: confirmed

| channel | overlap with the line, before | after |
|---|---|---|
| SCOUT — the arms | +0.364 | **+0.018** |
| NOVA — the bats | +0.132 | **−0.048** |
| ATLAS — the conditions | +0.569 | **+0.032** |
| VEGA — the price | −0.024 | −0.024 (nothing to remove) |
| **average across the three projectors** | **0.355** | **0.033** |

On games nobody had seen, the raw view is +0.283 overlapped with the line and the finished signal is **+0.001**.

The visible version of the claim, on 374 post-fence games: **old ATLAS is 63% mixed up with the line and hits 44.26%. New ATLAS is independent and hits 49.73%.** Same channel, same information, same games.

A parallel rebuild confirmed it independently. We re-instantiated three of the channels on a completely separate research track, reading their exact factor lists at import so they could not drift, changing only what they predict. Those rebuilt versions overlap the posted line at **−0.002 to 0.125** against the incumbents' 0.509 — and the conditions rebuild reads **51.0% on the same July games the incumbent read 43.2%.** Stripping out the line-shared part moved a July hit rate from 43.9% to 51.6%. The entire deficit lived in a part of the signal that was never its own.

### The accuracy claim: refused

**Zero of 150 candidates passed the four gates**, across 192 logged evaluations and 10 runs.

Per channel, on 8,644 games:

| channel | effect | range | t |
|---|---|---|---|
| SCOUT — arms | +0.0007 | −0.090 to +0.089 | **+0.02** |
| NOVA — bats | **+0.147** | **+0.054 to +0.239** | **+3.10** |
| ATLAS — conditions | −0.039 | −0.143 to +0.069 | −0.83 |
| VEGA — price | −0.099 | −0.191 to −0.010 | −2.10 |

A t-statistic of 0.02 on the arms channel is about as clean a zero as this program has produced — and it confirms an earlier reading on a sample 2.3 times larger.

The bats channel is the one real result: a genuine, positive, market-independent effect. It still fails adoption. It failed the head-to-head improvement gate. It passed the luck filter only on the bigger window and failed on the pre-declared primary one. And economically it does not clear: **52.34%, range 51.21% to 53.48%, against a 52.38% break-even.**

It is a measurable channel, not a profitable one, and that is exactly how we publish it.

### The candidate that passed, and then didn't

One price-channel variant cleared all four gates cleanly. Then the anti-trivial check — written before any of this existed — took it apart:

| what's actually in it | effect | t |
|---|---|---|
| the de-vigged market price **alone** | **+0.172** | **+3.64** |
| all price-level inputs | +0.141 | +2.97 |
| the full channel | +0.123 | +2.59 |
| **market structure only** (movement, disagreement, liquidity, staleness) | **−0.069** | **−1.47** |

The entire effect is the market echoing back at us. Strip the price level out and the channel's actual thesis — the thing that channel is *about* — is null to negative.

Two controls on the same games confirm the machinery is sound: pure noise came back at −0.022, and a line-only baseline at −0.081. Both null, as required.

### Two predictions we got wrong, published as wrong

We predicted that independent analysts would show *more* consistent month-to-month results. They did not — their monthly variation ran 13% to 26% above the pure-noise floor, where the old version ran at or below it. Reported as a failed prediction, not explained away.

The desk-decorrelation measure also regressed mildly, and the report gives the context rather than burying it: the failure this whole rebuild exists to prevent was 84–89% side agreement.

### A hypothesis killed by its own test

Screening 224 line-independent stats on an early window suggested a much better way to split the desk: the arms analyst looked systematically informative on *home-side* stats and the bats analyst on *away-side* stats. A plausible mechanism came with it — the home team does not bat in the bottom of the ninth when it is ahead.

Tested out of sample on 8,644 games, every side-restricted version collapsed, and the side-restricted bats analyst was **significantly worse** than the unrestricted one.

The report's own record of it: *my own hypothesis is dead, and it was killed by the test that was pre-registered to kill it.*

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
The general shape of this finding applies far beyond baseball.

**If you compare a small private estimate to a big public number, you are betting the big public number.** Our analysts' projections moved about 0.3 runs game to game; the posted total moves 1.12. Subtracting a rolling average *felt* like it removed the market from the decision, and it did remove the seasonal level — but not the game-by-game overlap, because the *inputs themselves* (park, pitching, weather) are the same inputs the market priced. The market's number is not an opponent standing outside your model. It is largely a projection of your own model's ingredients.

**The real damage is a record you cannot interpret.** Worse than being wrong. Two records at the same hit rate are not equally informative: an independent record measures its channel, while a tangled one measures its channel *plus the calendar*.

**Making it independent converts a lottery ticket into a truthful zero.** That is the honest summary of what this campaign bought. Accuracy did not improve. What improved is that when a channel now reads 50%, that 50% is a statement about the channel.

There is a matching limit on what you are allowed to *claim* once you predict the difference from the line, and it was written into the rules in advance. "Worse pitching means more runs" is known baseball physics and a fair assumption. "Worse pitching means more runs **than the market already expects**" is a claim about market inefficiency, and is not physics. The farm's version is sharper still: a model like this can claim a factor is *underpriced* and can never claim one is *overpriced*.

Finally, one rule amendment is on the record rather than hidden. A second threshold we set in advance turned out to be **badly specified** — a difference-based model's signal is about twenty times smaller, so that particular measure inflates automatically. It was dropped as a gate and kept as a description. The overlap threshold stands, and we cleared it.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
The four analysts kept their jobs — the arms, the bats, the conditions, the price. What changed is not what each one *reads*. It is what each one *bets*.

Each now asks whether its channel says this game is above or below **what the market is already pricing on that channel**, rather than above or below an average game.

The practical effect: analyst records became interpretable. When an analyst has a bad month now, that is information about the analyst rather than about which way the month's totals fell.

And the honest headline is the one in the report. Architecture improved decisively and measurably. Accuracy did not. Nothing was adopted on accuracy — refused by gates that were written before the numbers existed.

---

papers.title: Forget the Vig. Can Anyone Even Pick the Right Side?
papers.subtitle: We ignored the juice completely and asked the pure question: what's the best anyone can do picking over/under against a posted MLB total? The answer is 52.1%, and it belongs to the market.
papers.category: What We Know About the Market
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
Strip away the juice, the bet sizing, the price shopping — everything. Just ask the pure question: **what is the best anyone can do picking over or under against a posted MLB total?**

We wrote down the whole answer's shape before computing any of it: seven fully specified models, four free baselines on the identical games, 26 ways of slicing the data, a four-point confidence test, and — crucially — what we would conclude from a boring result.

On 8,412 games across 727 nights and four and a half seasons, the best of seven models reached **51.5%**, which is not statistically better than just betting the under every night. The best result achievable by *any* rule of any kind, including the free ones, was **52.1%** — obtained by copying the market's own de-vigged side.

Zero of seven models, zero of 26 splits and zero of the confidence tests survived. The two models with the most machinery in them were significantly **worse** than copying the price.

Break-even at standard juice is 52.4%. **The ceiling does not clear the juice.** That is why we do not promise you 60%, and it is the benchmark every other number on this site is measured against.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### The question, and why it's worth asking this way

It came from the product side, plainly: *maybe ignore the vig and figure out how to just pick over/under and win that.*

That is a good question, because it separates two things people usually tangle together. If a model cannot beat a coin flip on direction, no amount of price shopping saves it. If it *can*, the economics become a separate and much more solvable problem.

The whole plan was written down and cryptographically hashed before any result existed. The hash cited in the final report re-computes from disk and matches exactly, so nobody can claim the plan was adjusted afterward.

### The games

One row per game, decided **three hours before first pitch**. 10,372 games with a final, a total and a real price, spanning March 2022 to April 2026.

Pushes were dropped in advance — *a push is not a direction and cannot be hit* — at a measured 4.165% rate. Restricting to games where our simulator also had a number gives 9,168, and the declared warm-up period leaves **8,412 games across 727 nights** on which everything gets scored.

Every model and every baseline is scored on identical games. The rules state that a comparison on non-identical games is void.

### Seven models, declared in advance

Simple fundamentals. 98 stats with machine learning. The simulator alone. Market structure alone. Market price plus a fundamentals correction. Market price plus a simulator correction. Everything at once.

Settings were copied from existing production code and explicitly **not tuned** for this test. The stat lists were taken word-for-word from an earlier frozen report rather than re-picked. The pick rule was fixed in advance: over if the probability is above 50%, ties go under and still count, no sitting out.

### The bar was not a coin flip

This is the design choice that made the whole study meaningful.

The bar was: **beat whichever constant did better — always-over or always-under — with the constant allowed to pick its best side after the fact.**

The reason is in the rules, and the results confirmed it exactly. *The more one-sided a model is, the better it looks, and the one-sidedness is doing the work.* A model that "hits 54%" by riding a directional bias in the sample has not demonstrated accuracy.

The diagnostics prove the point. Our best model picked OVER only **30.34%** of the time, against a real over-rate of 49.394% — and agreed with the market's side 82% of the time. The simulator-only model picked over just **11.94%** of the time, and its entire advantage over always-under was 0.285 points. Against a 50% bar those would have looked interesting. Against the right bar, they are nothing.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
### The seven models

| model | accuracy | range | picks OVER |
|---|---|---|---|
| price + simulator correction | **51.510%** | 50.505 – 52.594 | 30.3% |
| price + fundamentals correction | 51.331% | 50.239 – 52.445 | 41.3% |
| market structure only | 51.296% | 50.297 – 52.328 | 36.3% |
| simple fundamentals | 50.892% | 49.805 – 51.945 | 38.5% |
| simulator only | 50.892% | 49.874 – 51.886 | 11.9% |
| everything, machine-learned | 50.297% | 49.199 – 51.337 | 44.8% |
| 98 stats, machine-learned | 50.131% | 49.042 – 51.212 | 44.2% |

Free baselines on the same games: **copy the market's side 52.116%**; bet the under 50.606%; coin flip 50.0%; bet the over 49.394%.

**Zero of seven survive.** And the two models with the most machinery — the 98-stat one and the everything one — are significantly *worse* than just copying the price.

Meanwhile the market's own side beats a coin flip decisively and beats the best constant clearly. The market is genuinely good. We are not.

### Does confidence help?

Keep only the games our best model feels surest about, and its accuracy goes 51.5% → 52.2% → 52.3% → **50.3%** → 51.6%. Flat, then it falls apart. Total range: 2.06 points. Pre-declared conclusion, written before any number existed: **our confidence is not informative.**

The market-only model is worse — its accuracy *collapses to 46.5%* on its own most confident tenth.

One model did produce a beautiful rising curve, up to **55.7%** on its most confident 5%. It was not promoted, and the reasons are both statistical and devastating. Pooling all three confidence curves as the rules required, the strongest result anywhere came in nowhere near the bar. And on those exact same most-confident games, **the market's own side hit 60.2%** — the model was 4.6 points *behind a free baseline* on the games it felt surest about.

The market's confidence curve, by contrast, rises properly: 52.1% → 52.3% → 52.4% → **54.2%**.

The conclusion in the report is exact: **the gradient that exists is a gradient in how predictable a game is, not in how much we know about it.** It is finding games that are easy for everyone. Being selective helps whoever has the best model — and that is not us.

### 26 ways of slicing the data

> Splits declared: 26. Splits tested: 26. Splits that survived: 0.

The best-looking was games where the favourite is between 5% and 12%, hitting 52.78% on 3,401 games — needing to clear a bar of 0.00385 and coming in at 0.0555. **Short by a factor of fourteen.** The flashiest, June games at 53.59%, is published uncorrected on purpose so it is on the record as mined and rejected.

Park groupings were cut on a pregame stat, never on outcomes. Thin cells were reported as insufficient and **still counted** against us, because dropping small cells after seeing them is the exact trick this whole protocol exists to block.

### The economics, as interpretation only

| price | you need | our best (51.51%) | the market's side (52.12%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| standard −110 | **52.381%** | short by 0.87 pt | short by **0.27 pt** |
| reduced −105 | 51.220% | +0.29 pt | +0.90 pt |
| very low −102 | 50.495% | +1.02 pt | +1.62 pt |
| best of 30+ books | ~50.6% | +0.9 pt | +1.5 pt |

That price table was declared in advance and is **interpretation only** — it never filtered a game, never selected a model, never entered a test.

The best-of-book row carries its own caveat, stated in the report: it is the maximum across 30-plus books at a single instant, restricted to the 72.1% of games where that best price sits on the same number the bet is defined on, and about 40% of the time the best price comes from one specific low-margin outlet.

And the reading that matters: **the vig was never the thing standing between us and a winning over/under bet. There is no directional accuracy here for the vig to eat.**

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
This is the most-quoted number in this program, so it is worth being exact about what it does and does not say.

**What it says.** On full-game MLB totals, decided three hours out, over 8,412 games and five seasons, no model we can build from the information available — including 98 stats with machine learning and a full physics simulator — picked sides better than a free constant. The ceiling on the whole exercise is 52.1%, and it belongs to the market. Break-even is 52.4%. **The ceiling does not clear the juice.**

**Why it will hold up.** The report makes an argument worth repeating: nulls under this protocol are the results *least* likely to be overturned by better data, because the failure is not "we lacked information." One model had 98 different stats and produced a coin flip. More capacity made it strictly worse — which is the signature of noise, not of a missing ingredient. Changing what we optimised for did not change the answer either.

**What it does not say.** It is not a claim that no edge exists anywhere in baseball betting. It is one bet type, one decision moment, one information set, one era. Derivative markets, in-game repricing and thin markets are separate questions, each tested separately in this program — mostly to the same answer, but on their own evidence.

**How it gets used.** This number is the yardstick for everything else. When a later study reports a channel at 52.34% with a range of 51.21% to 53.48%, this paper is what makes that legible: it is a genuine measurement, it is near the ceiling, and it still does not clear 52.38%. Without the ceiling, 52.34% is a hopeful number. With it, it is a precisely located one.

One detail here is worth stealing. The most extreme split we found — June at 53.59% — is published **uncorrected, deliberately**, so it is on the record as mined and rejected rather than quietly binned. That is the difference between a research programme and a marketing funnel. The funnel publishes June.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
This is why the site does not promise a 60% model, and why every record here is measured against a break-even number instead of against 50%.

It also explains something that would otherwise look strange: why so much of our engineering effort goes into **which games to bet, at which price, under which strategy** rather than into building a better totals model.

We measured the payoff from a better totals model directly. It is capped at 52.1%, and everything we can build sits below that cap. The only place value can still exist is in the decision layer — so that is where the work went.

---
