papers.abstract:
Every dead end this program has closed is a version of one sentence: **the market's number is set at the middle of what actually happens, and everything you could look up before first pitch is already inside it.**

This paper is the direct evidence, and it is uncomfortable.

We built the fundamentals model — pitching, parks, weather, bullpens, offences. On 9,562 games, the **posted total alone predicts runs more than twice as well** as our best version of it. And **adding our stats to the line makes the forecast worse**, not better, in both directions we tried.

We built a full physics simulator, validated it against the real distribution of baseball scores, and found that its median lands on the posted total **to within 0.02 runs**. Its added value over just reading the line is +0.00045.

We threw 50 player-form stats at it: significantly worse than the line alone, and getting worse each season.

And then we cheated. We handed a model the **actual roof state** — open or closed — which is information nobody had at the close. No edge. Zero of two tests passed. Betting the predicted-open games over returns −26.9%.

The market's entire advantage over a coin flip here is about a third of a thousandth of a point of forecast error — a tiny edge, extracted from an outcome that is roughly **96% unpredictable**. And it is already the best one available.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
Four independent lines of evidence, each written down in advance, each with no rewinding the tape, each measured against the market on identical games.

**Fundamentals against the line, as runs forecasts.** Three models — 8 stats, 18 stats, and 98 stats with machine learning — evaluated on 9,562 games, against the posted total used as a runs forecast, alone and combined.

**A physics simulator against the line, as a probability forecast.** Before we were allowed to compare it to a market, the simulator had to pass a fitness test against reality: variance within 3.4% of actual, skew and kurtosis within 0.023, the survival curve accurate to under 0.01 across the whole range from 2.5 to 20.5 runs, and a distributional test it comfortably passed. Only a simulator that reproduces real baseball is allowed to argue with a market.

**Shape, not just the average.** If the market's average is right but its implied *spread* is wrong, there is money in the tails. Tested two completely independent ways, with a kill threshold written down first.

**Public facts, with cheating allowed.** The strongest version of an efficiency test is to hand the model information it could not possibly have had. The roof study did exactly that: rather than predicting whether a retractable roof would be open, it used the **actual** roof state and asked whether the close had already priced it.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
### The line is the better runs model

| model | stats | how much run variation it explains |
|---|---|---|
| our 8-stat model | 8 | 1.46% |
| our 18-stat model | 18 | 1.85% |
| our 98-stat machine-learning model | 98 | **−2.02%** |
| **the posted total alone** | 1 | **4.16%** |
| the posted total + our 8 stats | 9 | 3.93% |
| the posted total + our 18 stats | 19 | 3.74% |

Two readings, both stated in the report. **The line is the better runs model** — more than twice as good as our best. And **adding fundamentals to the line makes the runs forecast worse, not better.**

The mechanism is direct: regress the line on our own projection and you recover **35% to 41%** of it. *We are rebuilding, noisily, a thing the market has already built precisely.*

And here is the part that stops this being a story about bad modelling. Our individual coefficients are not wrong. Per standard deviation, park factor is worth +0.375 runs, temperature +0.339, home starter ERA +0.220, home bullpen ERA +0.156. The baseball is real. It is simply already in the price.

### Where the market's edge lives, and how small it is

Four sentences carry the whole result.

**About 96% of a game's total runs is unpredictable.** The line explains 4.2% of it. The market's entire advantage over a coin flip on the over/under is about **0.00036** of forecast error.

**The closing total IS the fundamentals model.** Our stats reproduce 51% of the line and roughly 0.1% of what the line gets wrong. Every pitcher, park, weather and bullpen number we have is already in the posted number. Adding them on top moves the home starter's contribution by 0.45 percentage points and the team's batting average by 0.08.

**It's missing information, not bad calibration.** Our forecast quality runs 0.502 to 0.507 against the market's 0.524. Giving our model a free recalibration improves it — and it still loses, with a range that excludes zero.

**More capacity makes it worse.** 98 stats plus machine learning produces a *negative* result.

### Our own simulator agrees with the market

We ran four different versions of the simulator against the market's number. Nothing won. The best got within a whisker; the worst lost decisively.

But the physical result is more striking than the statistical one. **The simulator's median lands on the posted total to within 0.02 runs** — and within 0.06 for first-five-innings. Its added value over just reading the line is **+0.00045**. An independently constructed simulation of the sport, and a betting market, converge on the same number.

One derived warning is worth carrying with you, because it catches a lot of people. Average runs in a game are 8.92, but the *median* is 8, and totals average 8.446. So comparing the **average** to the line calls OVER on **75.4% of the card** — and hits 50.3%. That is the single easiest way to build a model that looks like an edge and is not.

### Shape closed on a ceiling, not a shrug

The tail-shape idea did not merely fail to reach significance. We measured its *maximum possible value*. Against a threshold set in advance, the ceiling on any shape correction is about **an order of magnitude below the bar.** A perfect oracle would miss it.

The mechanism explains why. A 1% error in the implied spread moves the over/under probability by about 0.00136, so you would need to be wrong about the spread by **14.7% game by game** to be worth two points of hit rate. Our simulator's spread is 98% determined by its own average, leaving an independent component that is 0.9% of the range. And **85.5% of de-vigged prices sit within two points of a coin flip** anyway, so there is barely any room where shape could matter.

The study also disarms a claim it could easily have made. The method you use to remove the vig moves the implied numbers by ±8%, which is *larger than any shape effect worth having* — so the tempting headline "the market is 11% too wide" is an artefact of the de-vigging method, not a finding.

### Public facts, with cheating allowed

The roof result is the cleanest single demonstration in the corpus. Given the **actual** roof state, there is no residual: zero of two tests pass, betting predicted-open games over returns **−26.9%**, and betting predicted-closed games under returns +2.4% while a dumb constant on the same games returns **+4.9%**.

> The close already absorbs roof information — even oracle knowledge of the actual roof state shows no residual.

Three more from the same family show the pattern is general.

A real behavioural effect, confirmed at overwhelming significance: totals drop **0.134 runs after a shutout**, with a t-statistic of −7.1. Fading that overreaction loses **8.4% on 2,426 bets**. The market's reaction is right-sized.

A first-inning scoring shade exists at half a point to a point of probability — about **five times too small** to pay the juice. Blind bets in either direction lose 5.2% and 6.7%.

Fifty player-form stats across 4,344 games made the forecast **significantly worse** than the line alone, with zero of six sub-tests surviving — and the damage growing every season: 2024 bad, 2025 worse, 2026 worst.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
This turns into a working rule that we now apply to every new idea: **if the fact is public and observable before first pitch, assume it is in the price, and require evidence to believe otherwise.** That rule has been tested dozens of times in these files and has not yet been wrong on a public fact.

Three consequences.

**Adding stats has almost no expected value here.** That is counterintuitive if your instinct is that a richer model wins. The measured relationship runs the other way: our 98-stat model is the *worst* of the three, and the 50-stat player-form composite is significantly worse than nothing. Where the true signal is tiny and 96% of the outcome is noise, extra capacity buys noise and nothing else.

**Rediscovering that a sharp market is well-priced is not a finding.** A model that reproduces the market's number, and scores well for it, has measured the market rather than beaten it. That is why every gate in this program strips the market's own number out before crediting anything.

**Where an edge could still live is now precisely specified.** If everything publicly knowable before first pitch is in the number, then edges — if any — live in what is *not* publicly knowable at the close, or in places where the market's plumbing rather than its information is broken. That is a far narrower and far more useful search than "build a better model."

The strongest thing about this result is *how* it was obtained. It was not inferred from a losing backtest. It was measured directly: by rebuilding the market's number from our own inputs and finding we recover 35 to 41% of it, by handing a model information it could not have had and finding no residual, and by computing the *maximum possible* value of a shape correction and finding it an order of magnitude below the bar. Those are constructive measurements, which is why the conclusion is stable.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
The number on the board is not a starting point to be improved. It is the best public estimate that exists, and we have measured exactly how good: better than anything we can build from public information, and made *worse* by adding our information to it.

That is why DiamondEdge does not claim to beat the closing line. We tested that claim about sixty-five different ways with pre-registered honest methods, and it is false for us in every market we can measure. The site says so.

It is also why the product's honest ambition is narrower and much more defensible: not a better forecast of runs, but a better **decision** about which of the market's own numbers to take, at which price, at which moment, under which strategy — with a public record of how that decision has actually done.

papers.title: We Found an 11.5% Edge on 496 Bets. Then We Killed It.
papers.subtitle: The most promising idea we ever tested. It survived three rebuilds and every economic check. It died when we stopped testing whether it made money and started testing whether it was true.
papers.category: What We Know About the Market
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
The most credible idea in sports betting is this: a sharp, low-margin book's price is close to fair value, so when a softer book's number drifts away from it, the sharp side is the right one. There is a published audited study behind it — 14 seasons, 31,247 flagged bets, +3.6% realised return.

We built it. Three times, each version written down in advance, each with sealed data held back.

It produced the best economics this program has ever measured: on one book, **496 bets across 272 days at 57.98% and +11.5% return**, with a range of +3.4% to +19.7% and every single economic check passing.

We retired it. The sealed data was never opened, and now never can be.

Here is why. At every version, the check we cared about most failed: **on our own flagged games, the sharp book's number forecast the outcome worse than the soft book's.** So we wrote a dedicated test of just the premise — no money, no thresholds, no strategy. Across all our bets, **the soft book's number was actually closer to the final total.**

The premise survives, weakly and not significantly, on exactly one book. And that book was chosen as best-of-fifteen **on return**, before any of this was measured.

Then the last piece fell in. The premise "worked" only at one specific point in the day — which happened to be the same point that carried the best returns. That looks like two independent confirmations. It was **one set of 162 bets, counted twice.**

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### Why it deserved three attempts

This was rated our highest-prior idea out of twelve, at 60–70% likely to show up in-sample and 35–45% likely to be deployable, on the strength of a large published audited study.

**Version 1** took the sharp book's de-vigged probability directly, translating between different posted totals with a simple distribution.

**Version 2** replaced that translation with a much smarter one, estimated separately for each range of totals — on the diagnosis that version 1's crude translation was the bottleneck.

**Version 3** changed the rule entirely: instead of "take the sharp side," it **blends** the two prices, with the blend weight frozen by a declared recipe and validated by leaving each season out in turn.

Every version was written down first, graded at real prices, run through the luck filter, and kept sealed data untouched.

### The check that decided everything

Alongside the money checks, each version carried a **premise check**: does the sharp book's number actually forecast the outcome better than the soft book's, on the specific games we flagged?

This is what separates a real edge from a lucky sample, and it is why this story has a clean ending. A profitable set of bets with a failing premise check is a set of bets that won — not a reason they should win.

### The falsifier

After version 3, instead of chasing the surviving economics, we wrote a test of *only* the premise. Its measure is deliberately simple: for each flagged game, compare how far the sharp book's number was from the actual total against how far the soft book's number was.

Negative means the sharp book was closer, which is what the whole idea requires.

The falsifier reproduced version 3's populations **exactly** — same frozen settings, same 496-bet take set, same 834-game flag set — so its verdict applies to the actual bets, not to an approximation of them.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
### The economics: genuinely good

| what | bets (days) | hit | return | range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **one book, primary threshold** | **496 (272)** | **57.98%** | **+11.5%** | **+3.4% to +19.7%** |
| same book, bigger gaps | 277 (186) | 58.49% | +12.2% | +1.2% to +23.1% |
| same book, biggest gaps | 153 (115) | 62.50% | +20.4% | +6.2% to +35.3% |
| a three-book retail cluster | 820 (344) | 53.58% | +3.1% | −4.2% to +10.3% |
| all books, price-gated | 8,557 | — | +4.6% | −0.2% to +9.4% |

The controls on the headline cell rule out the obvious explanations: always-over on the same games returns −7.1% and always-under −1.6%. This is not a directional bias in disguise.

### The premise check: failed at every version

| version | soft book's forecast quality | the claim's forecast quality | who won |
|---|---|---|---|
| v1 — take the sharp side | 0.24981 | 0.25137 | **soft book** |
| v2 — with a smarter translation | 0.24977 | 0.25142 | **soft book** |
| v3 — blend the two | 0.24977 | 0.24816 | claim, but not significantly |

The version 2 result is the informative one. The entire point of version 2 was to fix version 1's diagnosis that the crude translation was the problem. Making the translation genuinely sophisticated changed the answer by **0.00005**. The version 1 diagnosis is falsified. The failure is structural.

But version 2 did establish something real, and it is the one thing we kept. Blending the two prices produces a genuine minimum in forecast error at **40% of the way** from the soft book toward the sharp one — not at 100%. And the divergence signal **overshoots by about 2.5×**: the average flagged gap is 9 points of probability while the real edge is 3–4.

That is a genuine, reusable fact about market structure. It is also a warning, because a signal that overshoots 2.5× produces exactly the confident-looking, occasionally-spectacular flags that a search will latch onto.

### The falsifier: the premise came out backwards

| population | bets | result | which way |
|---|---|---|---|
| the one book, all flagged games | 834 | −0.0540 | sharp closer, not significant (p = 0.07) |
| **the one book, its 496 actual bets** | **496** | **−0.0413** | **sharp closer, nowhere near significant (p = 0.23)** |
| a second retail book, its bets | 723 | +0.0062 | **soft book closer** |
| all bettable US books, their bets | 4,886 | +0.0558 | **soft book closer** |
| all target books, their bets | 8,557 | +0.0510 | **soft book closer** |

On our own bets, the premise does not hold — and across the full universe it holds in **reverse**.

Three more diagnostics closed the case.

**The timing is wrong.** The effect exists only at one hour out and is flat or slightly reversed at three and six hours. One hour out is *also* the slice that carried the best returns — the **identical 162 bets**. The "mechanism" and the "profit" were not two pieces of evidence. They were one slice counted twice.

**The stability is wrong.** Three of five seasons come out with the sign the wrong way, and the whole effect concentrates in one stretch of 49 bets over 20 days — which is the exact +31.2% return slice that made this thread look alive in the first place. Exclude the last two seasons and the sign flips.

**The concentration is wrong.** Across 496 bets, the total advantage is 20.5 runs, and the most extreme 10% of rows carry about **4.1 times the entire net effect**. 45.2% of rows go the other way. This is not a broad edge. It is a handful of outliers.

The controls behave exactly as they should: on non-flagged games from the same book, the measure sits at essentially zero across 7,373 rows. The machinery is not producing a false sign.

### The selection problem, named

The one book on which the premise weakly survives is the book that was **chosen as best-of-fifteen on return before any of this was measured**. The report says so without cushioning: that is the selection problem restated in forecast-accuracy space.

And the +10.7%, +11.4% and +11.5% figures that recur across three versions and a literature review are the **same slice**. They must not be presented as three independent confirmations.

For scale: 0.04 runs is about **one percent of a typical miss**, since both books are off by roughly 3.5 runs on an average game.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
This is our fourth honoured stop, and the most expensive one. The idea is retired. The planned live census was not run. The forward registration was not written. And the sealed six-week window was **never opened at any stage** — the only agreed route to opening it closed with the idea.

The falsifier's own justification is the line to take away: **a premise that cannot be demonstrated on 496 of our own bets is not a premise to spend seasons on.**

Three lessons.

**Test the mechanism, not the money.** Every version of this had passing economics and a failing premise. If the premise check had not been declared as blocking in advance, the natural path is obvious: ship the profitable book-specific cell, watch it regress, and spend a season explaining why. The check that killed this was designed to kill it, before the profitable slice existed.

**Selecting on a subgroup is invisible from inside the subgroup.** The headline cell has 496 bets, 272 days, a passing luck filter, passing controls and a range clear of zero. Every one of those is a genuine check, and not one of them can see that the **book** was chosen on return from fifteen candidates before the analysis began. That choice sits upstream of every statistic computed downstream of it.

**Beware evidence that is one observation wearing two hats.** The single most persuasive moment in the whole programme was that the mechanism was strongest at exactly the point in the day where the money was best. That looks like convergent validation from two directions. It was 162 bets, counted twice.

There is a positive result buried here that we kept. The 2.5× overshoot, and the finding that the right blend weight is about 40% rather than 100%, is a genuine, reusable measurement of how far to trust a cross-book divergence. Independent outside work found the same shape from a different angle, reporting that on large model-versus-sharp disagreements the sharp side won about 77% of head-to-heads and the model was anti-calibrated *specifically on disagreement games*.

So the standing rule in this program is now: **a big disagreement with a sharp market is a reason NOT to bet, not a reason to bet.** A parallel campaign sharpened it further, confirming three separate times that a divergence in your favour at a retail book is information about what the book knows, not a gift.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
DiamondEdge does not ship a cross-book divergence product, despite having built one that returned +11.5% on 496 graded bets with every economic check passing.

That is the clearest illustration of how this operation works. The number was real. The bets were graded at real prices. The range cleared zero. And the premise underneath it did not survive being tested on its own terms — so we retired the idea, and left sealed the data that could have been spent proving it.

What survives is the honest residue: a measured 2.5× overshoot on divergence signals, a standing rule that disagreeing with a sharp market is a veto rather than an edge, and a documented example of what a selection effect looks like from the inside — which is to say, exactly like a finding.

papers.title: The Minor Leagues: Ten Prospect Analysts Who Can't Get Promoted By Getting Hot
papers.subtitle: A leaderboard of ten models always has a leader. After a month one of them will be sitting at 56% and it'll be noise. So we built the promotion system to physically ignore the leaderboard.
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
A leaderboard of ten models always has a leader. After a month one of them will be sitting at 56% and it will be noise.

Our research farm is ten prospect analysts — seven brand new angles on a baseball total, three rebuilds of existing channels — and the whole thing is designed around that problem. **Leading the leaderboard is not what earns promotion**, and that is enforced structurally rather than promised.

The promotion function has no parameter that could receive a ranking, verified by inspecting its own signature. It never imports the leaderboard, verified by inspecting its own source code. And a test fixture that leads the board at 60.4% is asserted **unpromotable**.

The first month's leaderboard shows exactly why all that is necessary: **two of ten prospects have ranges that exclude a coin flip, in opposite directions.** One at 56.0%, one at 44.0%. That is what ten coin flips look like.

The honest timeline, computed before any prospect had a single read: the earliest anyone can clear the bar is **late September to October 2026.**

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### The ten

Seven brand new angles, each answering a question the four main analysts do not:

| | Title | The idea |
|---|---|---|
| **RELAY** | THE TIRED PEN | how many bullpen innings this game demands, against how much bullpen is left |
| **BAROMETER** | THE MAN BEHIND THE PLATE | grades the umpire and nothing else |
| **CIRCUIT** | THE SCHEDULE | rest, city changes, how deep into the grind each team is |
| **TAPE** | WHAT MOVED, AND WHAT DIDN'T | the total moving while the moneyline sits still |
| **CHALK** | THE OTHER TWO MARKETS | reading the run line and moneyline as a clue about the total |
| **SWING** | VARIANCE, NOT AVERAGE | how volatile the two offences are; every factor a contrast, never a level |
| **ANVIL** | BALLS IN PLAY | how much contact there is and how hard it's hit |

Plus three rebuilds — **FORGE, HARVEST and PRISM** — which are the arms, bats and conditions analysts' *exact* stat lists and *exact* factor tables, read at import so they cannot drift apart, with precisely one thing changed: what they predict.

Where an incumbent predicts total runs, these predict **runs relative to the posted total** — which means they ask the honest question: *is this game above what the market is already pricing on my channel?*

Those three exist because of what we found in the incumbents: their signal was 51% the same as the posted total, so their records were partly just a bet on which way the month's totals fell. The rebuilds overlap the line at **−0.002 to 0.125**, against the incumbents' 0.509 — and the conditions rebuild reads **51.0% on the same July games the incumbent read 43.2%.**

### Two fences, not one

Training stops at the end of June, like the main analysts.

The farm then adds a **stricter fence on 1 August**, and the reason is subtle but important: the ten ideas were **chosen** on 1 August by someone who had already read July.

So July is *clean evidence about a model* and *spent evidence about a choice*. The leaderboard shows July. The promotion gate refuses it — and a test fixture proves that a spectacular July-only record counts for exactly zero.

### The bar

Eight gates, all blocking. Only reads after the second fence count. It has to be profitable with a range excluding zero, with **nights resampled, never games**. It has to survive the luck filter across all fourteen candidates — ten prospects plus the four incumbents, because a prospect is competing for a seat an incumbent holds — and the function **errors out on a family of any other size**, so the denominator cannot be quietly shrunk. It has to beat matched constants *and* the market's own forecast accuracy, and not be more than 80% one-sided. It has to survive deleting its single best bet, and deleting its single best night. It needs 60 reads across 20 nights. And it needs a written plan whose file timestamp predates the scoring.

Clearing all of it writes a **proposal**. Entering the main four requires a human to sign a file whose hash matches the candidate. **The nightly system does not have the promotion function available to it and cannot call it.**

### Four locks that a prospect read is never a bet

Every row is flagged as not a pick, with a helper that errors out on any bet-shaped field. The farm can only write to its own files. Its record is a leaf on the payload that no pick builder reads.

And a structural check verifies no farm name appears in the pick path — a check that caught a real collision on its very first run, when a prospect originally named SPREAD clashed with an existing record key. It was fixed by renaming the prospect to CHALK.

The proof is a checksum, building the payload twice in one process with the farm on and off: **all 411 history and 20 live pick objects hash identically**, and the farm's own record is the only key whose value moves. Cost to the payload: 87.7 KB, or 1.37%.

**Two of ten have ranges that exclude a coin flip, in opposite directions. That is what ten coin flips look like, and it is why rank earns nothing.** The last column — the only one that matters for promotion — is zero all the way down.

### The prospect that files nothing

RELAY had **all seven of its factors refused by the data**: every bullpen-fatigue factor came out pointing the opposite way to its declared physics. Because factors are locked to their declared direction, every one was driven to exactly zero, the signal is identically zero, and RELAY writes no reads at all.

The interpretation is better than the outcome. When you are predicting *the difference from the posted line*, declaring a direction claims a factor is both real **and underpriced**. RELAY's zero therefore says: **the market prices bullpen fatigue at least as hard as RELAY does.** That is a result about the market, not an outage — and the leaderboard renders it as a sentence rather than as an empty row.

### An idea we were asked for, and declined

The brief called for an eleventh prospect testing whether a channel might be not weak but *backwards*.

We refused to build it, on measurement. Tested on the training window rather than on the July record that raised the idea, the conditions channel is worth **−0.014 runs with a t-statistic of −0.09** and an own-side hit rate of 49.8%. There is nothing to invert, and building it would have spent a fourteenth of the family's error budget on a hypothesis already known to be false. The refutation is published on the payload rather than buried, and sits on a registry of declined directions so it cannot be quietly re-proposed.

Three more directions are on that registry with reasons: cross-book disagreement (retired), first-five-innings dynamics (closed twice), and defensive quality — for the honest reason that **there is no fielding data in this repository at all.**

### When this can honestly conclude

Computed in advance, before any prospect accrued a single read.

A prospect with a genuine 3-point edge — 55.4% against a 52.4% break-even — makes about 0.06 units per read against a per-read swing of about 1.0. Grading by nights rather than games roughly doubles the error bar. So it needs roughly **250 to 350 nights** for a range that excludes zero.

The luck filter makes it harder: with fourteen candidates, the best prospect needs to be about a 2.7-sigma result rather than a 2-sigma one, costing about another 40% in sample.

Conclusion, stated in advance: **somewhere around late September to October 2026.** The sample-size gate on its own is reachable in about three weeks at fifteen games a night — which is exactly why it is not the only gate.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
The farm exists because of a specific, recurring failure. Research groups generate lots of candidates, rank them, promote the top one, and then discover that ranking is itself a selection procedure with no statistical control attached.

The usual remedy proposed is "apply a correction to the leaderboard." Ours is stronger: **remove ranking from the promotion path entirely, and verify by code inspection that it cannot get back in.**

Two ideas worth taking elsewhere.

**Separate evidence about a model from evidence about a choice.** This is what the second fence is for, and it is subtle. July is perfectly good out-of-sample evidence about how each prospect's *model* performs, because the models were fenced at June. It is *spent* evidence about **which ten ideas got chosen**, because the person choosing had read July. Most research pipelines have one fence and quietly conflate the two.

**A trustworthy zero beats an ambiguous record.** The three rebuilt channels will very likely land near 50%. That is the intent. Making a signal independent of the market converts a lottery ticket into a truthful zero — and a model that answers a real question and lands at 50% is a far better object than one whose record was decided by which way the month's totals fell.

The report states the whole point without overclaiming: the value is not that one of them wins. It is that ten real questions now get answered on a clean forward window, with a bar that a lucky month cannot clear — and that the answer *no* arrives with a range attached instead of a shrug.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
The farm is visible as a research surface and never as a pick. Every prospect read carries a flag saying it is not a bet, its files are fenced away from every pick builder, and the whole block was proved inert by rebuilding the payload twice in one process and hashing all 431 pick objects.

What you can watch is a real research process happening in public: ten stated ideas, each with a plan written before it took a single read, each accruing evidence against a bar published in advance, with a stated date by which the question becomes answerable.

When one of them clears — or, more likely, when all ten do not — the answer will arrive with a range attached and a human signature required before anything on your board changes.

papers.title: Shadows, Jet Lag and Network Theory: Eight Wild Ideas, One Wall
papers.subtitle: Exact solar astronomy. Published sleep science. A neural net reading the raw quote tape. AI mining our own failures. All eight hit the same wall the boring models hit.
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
After roughly seventy ordinary ideas had closed as dead ends, we ran a deliberately weird round. Eight instruments, all borrowed from outside sports analytics.

Network science on the season's matchup graph. A neural network reading the raw multi-book quote tape. Published circadian and workload physiology. Exact solar astronomy with zero fitted parameters. Information theory over the pattern of how runs arrive. Forecasting the closing line itself. Stacking every model we own. And a multi-agent AI pipeline mining our own accumulated failures for mechanisms nobody had proposed.

Eight nulls, two blocked, nothing that worked — with every instrument landing on the same market reference number.

Two of the nulls are genuinely *informative* rather than just underpowered. The jet-lag study had an **87.5% chance of catching the effect** it was looking for, and did not — and the factors do not predict raw runs either, so it is not that the market got there first. The shadow study used astronomy with no fitted parameters, so overfitting was structurally impossible, and found that betting high-shadow games under **loses to a dumb constant**.

And the round's single most valuable output was not a signal at all. It was discovering that roughly **45–47% of games in a 19.2-million-row odds archive carried another game's prices.**

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
Every front was written down in advance with its own kill thresholds. Every one trained only on games that had already finished. Every one was compared to the market on identical games.

**Matchup network cycles.** Treat the season as a network of who beat whom and by how much, and extract the *intransitive loops* — the A-beats-B, B-beats-C, C-beats-A patterns that a simple team-strength rating cannot represent.

**A neural net on the raw tape.** A recurrent network with seven per-event inputs and a learned book identity, reading up to 160 quote changes per game across as many as 25 books, three random seeds averaged. Train on 2021, predict 2022; train on 2021 and 2022, predict 2023. The question: given the *raw sequence* rather than hand-built stats, can a learner find something we missed?

**Circadian rhythms and workload.** Published sleep-science parameters, frozen before any result was read: body clock shifts forward at 1.0 hour a day and back at 1.5, a seven-day half-life, and workload decay of two days for catchers and three for starters. Applied to travel, time zones and start times.

**Solar geometry.** A shadow-severity score built from real solar-position mathematics with **zero fitted parameters**, cross-checked against a completely independent implementation to within 0.05 degrees of direction and 0.4 degrees of height.

**Scoring-sequence patterns.** Information-theory measures over pitching and scoring sequences, on the idea that the *pattern* of how runs arrive carries something the totals lose.

**Forecast the close.** Predict where the line will settle, and bet the predicted drift early.

**Stack everything.** A model on top of eight of our own models, with one specific co-headline hypothesis: that games where our models *disagree* most are the games the market is most likely to have wrong.

**AI archaeology.** Twelve independent AI sessions, each forced through a different expert lens, reading roughly seventy of our closed dead ends and a data inventory — with **zero game results and zero prices** in any prompt — proposing mechanisms, which were then ranked and tested as ordinary statistics.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
### The scoreboard

| front | verdict | the headline |
|---|---|---|
| sun and shadow geometry | NULL | 651 high-shadow games; betting them under returns −1.28% against a constant's +2.35% |
| circadian and workload | NULL (informative) | zero of six factors survive; 87.5% power |
| matchup network cycles | NULL | the cycle model is significantly *worse* than the market |
| scoring-sequence patterns | NULL | zero of five; out-of-sample performance actually *falls* |
| neural net on the raw tape | NULL | 48.6% direction accuracy; never produces a confident prediction |
| stack everything | NULL | model disagreement doesn't predict market error at all |
| forecast the close | NULL | betting the predicted drift early loses 3.5–4.8 cents per dollar to the juice |
| AI archaeology | NULL | passed the statistical screen; lost 1.29 points on economics |
| AI as a handicapper | NULL | 0.26293 forecast error against the market's 0.24890 |
| AI reading news | BLOCKED | infrastructure |

### Two nulls that actually close a question

**Jet lag.** Most nulls in this space are underpowered — you find nothing because you could not have found anything. This one is different. It had an **87.5% chance** of detecting an effect worth about 0.58 runs, across 4,486 paired games. Zero of six factors survived the luck filter, with the strongest coming nowhere near.

And the second half is what makes it conclusive: **it is not that the market had already priced it. The factors do not predict raw runs scored either.** The strongest one is worth about 0.076 runs per standard deviation, statistically indistinguishable from zero.

There was plenty of exposure to find, if it existed: 32.3% of games carry some body-clock misalignment, 419 of them at three hours or more. The high-dose games came in at 50.4% over against a market-implied 49.9%. And there is no dose-response — more jet lag does not mean more effect.

The report's own summary: *this design would have caught that about 88% of the time. It did not.*

**Shadows.** Zero fitted parameters means overfitting is structurally impossible. This is astronomy, not statistics. Across 3,499 eligible open-air games with 651 in the high-shadow class, every test fails — and the economics give the clean answer: betting those games under at the best closing price returns **−1.28%**, while a dumb always-under on the same eligible games returns **+2.35%**.

A verified sun-position engine says high-shadow games do not run under. The effect is smaller than the broadcast lore and already worthless at the close.

### Two nulls that close a methodological door

**The neural net on the raw tape** answers a standing objection: *maybe your inputs are wrong.* Given the raw quote sequence rather than hand-built statistics, a learner produced a forecast slightly worse than the market at both decision points, and — most tellingly — **direction accuracy of 48.6%**, below a coin flip. Its confidence bucket was empty because the model **never** produces a probability more than 0.059 away from a coin flip.

The conclusion: it is not that we encoded the wrong inputs. A learner given the raw sequence could not find any encoding that works either.

**The stack** answers a different standing objection: *maybe your models are individually weak but jointly strong, especially where they disagree.* Its co-headline hypothesis was tested directly, before any betting rule: the correlation between how much our models disagree and how wrong the market is comes to **+0.011, p = 0.61.**

Games where our models split hardest are simply not games the market misses. And the member models are genuinely different from each other, so this is not a lack-of-diversity failure. The full eight-model stack scored *worse* than the market.

### The graph result, and why one number is the whole story

The network-derived total correlates **0.456** with the closing line — a substantial, real relationship.

The correlation of its *disagreement with the line* with what actually happened: **0.019.**

And the disagreement predicts the outcome *worse* in high-cycle games than in low-cycle ones, which is precisely backwards from the hypothesis. The cycle model comes out significantly worse than the market.

That pattern — a feature that reproduces about half the line and none of its error — is the recurring signature of this entire corpus, showing up here from network science.

### The keeper

The round's most valuable single output was a data bug.

The neural-net front needed clean per-event quote sequences, and in building them discovered that a 19.2-million-row historical odds archive was keying prices to game IDs without verifying the event: **59% of 2021–2023 games carry more than two hours of listing spread, and roughly 2.43 million rows (47%) belonged to a listing other than the game played.**

That triggered a full audit, a rebuild of the identity layer across all 19,192,231 rows, fixes to the collector and the live feed and the serving path, and an honest re-flagging of roughly a dozen previously banked nulls as no longer informative.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
The synthesis puts the round's conclusion in two sentences worth quoting exactly:

> Eight genuinely new instruments — network science, a raw-tape neural net, published sleep physiology, exact astronomy, sequence-information theory, close forecasting, full-program stacking, and LLM archaeology over our own failures — all found the same wall the conventional models found.

> New instruments did not find daylight; they found the same efficient price from eight new angles. The box was never the problem. The market is the box.

Three things make this round worth more than its scoreboard suggests.

**Agreement from unrelated directions is strong evidence.** One null is a failure. Eight nulls from eight methodologically unrelated instruments, all landing on the same reference, is a measurement of the *market* rather than a measurement of us. Each front could have failed for its own idiosyncratic reason. They did not fail idiosyncratically.

**Power matters more than significance.** A null with an 87.5% chance of catching the effect closes a question. A null with a 20% chance postpones it. The jet-lag study's power calculation, done in advance, is what turns "we found nothing" into "there is nothing here above about half a run" — and its extra check on raw runs rules out the alternative explanation that the market simply got there first.

**Weird instruments are worth running precisely because they are cheap and closable.** Each of these cost days, not seasons, and each closed a door permanently. A shadow effect, a jet-lag effect, a scheduling-network effect and a scoring-pattern effect are all things a competitor may still be quietly hoping for. We measured them, published the numbers, and moved on.

Two reports in this round carry self-flagged caveats that get reproduced wherever they are cited: one front's builder took an early exploratory look before the confirmatory run, so its results are marked as weakened; and the AI pipeline was run through a substituted tool after an authentication failure, written down before generating anything. Neither was quietly re-run into a cleaner-looking result.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
Nothing from this round ships, and that is the intended outcome for eight of ten fronts.

What changes is what happens next time somebody suggests that a model should account for shadows in day games, or jet lag on a coast-to-coast trip, or the loop structure of the season's matchups, or the shape of how runs arrived last week.

The answer is not a shrug. It is a report with a sample size, a power calculation and a range — and in the case of shadows and jet lag, a null from a design that was strong enough to have found the thing if it were there.

And a system that tested eight exotic instruments and published eight nulls is a system whose surviving claims were not chosen by which ones happened to look good.

papers.title: Everything That Didn't Work — and Why We Show You All of It
papers.subtitle: Roughly seventy ideas tested and killed, with the numbers attached. Including the ones that looked spectacular. Including fourteen of our own published results that we later took back.
papers.author: KytePush Research
tags: we took our own results back
papers.abstract:
Most quantitative claims in sports betting are unfalsifiable, for one boring reason: only the winners are ever shown. If you cannot see how many ideas were tried, you cannot tell a real edge from the luckiest survivor of an unreported search.

We invert that. Roughly **seventy mechanisms have been tested and closed** in this program, and every one is published with its numbers, its sample, its range and its verdict — including several that looked outstanding right up until they were tested properly.

This paper is the ledger. It covers a systematic hunt that took 97 ideas down to 12 tests and zero survivors. Effects that are real, overwhelming, and still unprofitable. A mechanism we did not merely fail to confirm but actively **disproved**, with the same wrong-direction result reproduced on a second book. A live in-game repricing engine beaten by a constant. And a statistically significant finding we refused because the significance was not the whole story.

It also covers the hardest category: **about fourteen of our own banked nulls that we withdrew** after auditing the data underneath them.

The argument is simple. A shop that publishes its failures is a shop whose successes mean something, because you can see the denominator.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
Every entry here meets the same standard a positive result would: written down before the data was read, evaluated with no rewinding the tape, graded at real prices through the economic gate or explicitly labelled as a flat-juice convention, measured by resampling whole nights, and corrected for how many things we tested.

A dead end only earns a place in this ledger if it is **informative** — meaning the design had enough power to have found the effect if it existed. Dead ends that fail that test get recorded as **BLOCKED** rather than closed, and several are.

The ledger is public. Of 89 tracked research items on our roadmap, **32 carry a closed-dead-end status**.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
### 97 ideas, 12 tests, zero survivors

One research round shows the discipline end to end. It started with **97 raw ideas**, de-duplicated to 36, of which **12 were built** — each written down first, each on development data only.

**Nothing survived. Zero of the twelve earned real money. Nine doors are now closed for good.**

The synthesis's own explanation of why is the most useful sentence in it: the places that looked like free money turn out to be either **informed behaviour by the books** or noise; and where a real pattern was found — and several were — the price already had it baked in.

| what we tested | what happened |
|---|---|
| shading the same total across books | zero of ten survive; the key-total over cell returns −22.7% |
| scanning against a sharp book's fair price | zero of ten; and the effect *decays by year*: +20.7% in 2021 down to −7.2% in 2026 |
| following stale sharp moves | nine of nine dead; the ungated version loses 4.4% on 4,145 bets |
| checking a book's internal coherence | premise failed both ways; zero of seven |
| following the first book to move | the effect is REAL — that book moves first 43% of the time, ~3× the sharp book — and betting it lost 22.7% on 19 takes |
| first-inning market softness | the shade is real and about 5× too small; blind bets lose 5.2% and 6.7% |
| roof-decision timing | zero of two; betting predicted-open games over returns −26.9% |
| fading post-shutout overreaction | the shading is CONFIRMED at −0.134 runs, t = −7.1; fading it loses 8.4% on 2,426 bets |
| joint bullpen state | zero of five; the mirror side came out wrong-signed |

A bookkeeping correction is in the same synthesis, and we leave it in: one front arrived tagged as a survivor while its own report said dead end. *The report is authoritative; the tag was wrong.*

### Real effects that don't pay — the most instructive category

Three of those entries are the most useful results in this whole program, because they are not failures to find an effect. They are *successes* at finding one.

**The post-shutout drop.** Totals fall 0.134 runs after a shutout, with a t-statistic of −7.1 — an overwhelming, unmistakable pattern in how books move their numbers. Fading it loses **8.4% on 2,426 bets**. The market's reaction is real and correctly sized.

**The first-mover effect.** One book genuinely moves first about 43% of the time, roughly three times as often as the sharp reference. Two separate measurements of the follow-on effect both passed the luck filter. Betting on it lost **22.7%**.

**The first-inning shade.** It exists, measurably, at half a point to a point of probability. The juice is about five times that.

The lesson those three share: **a statistically overwhelming pattern in market behaviour is not the same thing as a bet, and the gap between them is usually the juice.**

### A mechanism disproved, not merely unproven

The strongest form of a negative result is not "we couldn't confirm it." It is "we confirmed the opposite."

One study got there. Its premise was that persistent gaps between a retail book and a sharp book mean the retail book is mispriced. Result: zero of six, with the persistent-gap cell at **−11.33%** against a transient cell at −0.85%.

And the mechanism came out **reversed**: on persistent-gap games **the retail book's number is 0.035 runs closer to the final total** than the sharp book's. The pattern is negative at all four book-and-timing combinations, and the wrong-direction result was **reproduced independently on a second book**.

The report says it plainly — *the mechanism is refuted, not merely unproven* — and draws the general conclusion: **a divergence in your favour at a retail book is information about what the book knows, not a gift.**

### A live engine beaten by a constant

Live in-game repricing was a well-resourced front with a validated simulator and a 19.2-million-row ground-truth store. Result: **6,508 bets, −3.24% return**, minus 210.8 units. Blind over and blind under both lose about 6%. Zero of four subgroups survive. Our simulator flagged an edge on 51.5% of eligible quotes at a median claimed edge of 7.7%.

Two diagnostics closed it properly. Assuming perfect execution, the forecast gap is borderline; assuming *real* execution, it is decisively negative, with only **38% same-number fills** and a median line move of a full run.

And the sentence that settles it: **a constant "always 50%" baseline nearly ties the de-vigged market and beats our simulator.** Because it is a signal problem rather than a speed problem, faster execution rescues nothing. Do not build live infrastructure on this result.

### A significant finding, correctly refused

Not every dead end is a zero. One study asked whether our model's own confidence sorts its picks by trustworthiness — and found that it does: a real ordering with **p = 0.005**, running from 48.2% in the bottom decile to 54.8% in the top.

We refused it anyway, and the reasons are the interesting part.

The declared shrink clause fired, because the flagged cell was too thin. The flagged slice is **94.5% one-sided**, against a declared band of 25–75%. Its calibration test fails. And the pre-declared "avoid the worst picks" veto rule came out **backwards** — the games it would have vetoed returned **+6.4%**, with a range clear of zero.

A less disciplined process ships the significance and quietly omits the sidedness.

### The hardest entries: our own

The most uncomfortable rows in this ledger are results we withdrew.

An audit of a 19.2-million-row historical odds archive found that prices had been keyed to game IDs without verifying the event — so in the most affected extraction pattern, more than a fifth of quote cells were contested between two different ballgames and **the wrong game's listing won 99.7% of the contests**.

The accounting was published in both directions. **No banked positive conclusion rested on it — every exposed study had already published a null.** But roughly **fourteen of about seventy** of those nulls had tested their idea against a market anchor that was the wrong game's number for about half the sample. Those are not informative nulls. They were re-flagged in public, with the reason attached.

The symmetric statement is also published: some of those might have been *positives*, and we cannot know without re-running. We do not get to keep only the convenient half of that sentence.

### Blocked, not closed

Several fronts are honestly labelled unanswered rather than answered.

A pitcher-scratch study found only 45% of flagged scratches were real, against a 90% gate — and just 10 true scratches in 4.3 seasons. Not enough to test. A team-total ladder front is blocked with 41 collected games and zero outcomes, waiting on a trigger with a projected date. A first-five-innings front returned a clean null; the run-line front was blocked on a fitness failure the simulator's own diagnostics caught.

And a platoon-splits study closed at 176 games with a **50.57% hit rate against a 50.66% break-even** — *directionally right, 0.09 points short of paying for itself, and nowhere near distinguishable from noise* — with its sealed data left unspent.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
The case for publishing failures is usually made on scientific grounds. Here it is also the main commercial argument, so it is worth saying directly.

**You cannot judge a winner without knowing the denominator.** A 55% strategy on 500 bets is meaningless if it is the best of two thousand searched. We publish the searches: 2,848 strategies in one tournament, 97 ideas in one hunt, 150 candidate evaluations in one rebuild, 26 declared splits in the ceiling study. When something survives here, you can see what it survived.

**Dead ends are constraints, and constraints compound.** Each closed door narrows where an edge could possibly be. After roughly seventy closures, the remaining space is precisely specified rather than vaguely hopeful: not "build a better model," but "find something that is either not publicly knowable at the close, or where the market's plumbing rather than its information is broken." That is a far more useful research programme than the one this started as.

**A dead end that turns out to rest on bad data has to be withdrawn as loudly as a winner would be.** This is the test of whether a failure ledger is a real instrument or a marketing device. A dead end we cite as a reason not to pursue something is a load-bearing claim. Fourteen of ours came down.

**"We tested X and the market had it priced" is a much stronger statement than silence.** It tells you the question was asked, how hard, and with how much power. It is also, unavoidably, an invitation to check our arithmetic — which is the point.

The general shape of everything here is one sentence, and every closed door is a variation of it: **the market's number is set at the middle of what actually happens, and everything you could look up before first pitch is already inside it.**

papers.title: We Cheated On Purpose: Does Knowing the Lineup Actually Help?
papers.subtitle: Instead of trying and failing to beat the market on lineups, we handed a model the ACTUAL nine who played — information nobody had — and measured the absolute best case. There isn't one.
papers.author: KytePush Research
papers.abstract:
"Knowing the lineup before the market reacts" is one of the most intuitive edges in baseball betting. This paper closes it, with a method stronger than the usual one.

Instead of trying to extract the edge and failing — which proves nothing, because maybe we extracted it badly — we measured the **absolute ceiling** by cheating. We handed a model the actual nine players who batted, which is information nobody had at any point before first pitch, and asked how much better it could possibly do.

The answer: a much better *actual* lineup is worth +0.125 runs once you account for the posted total, and the *projected* lineup already captures **+0.114 of that.** The surprise — what perfect foresight adds over what everyone already knew — is worth **+0.019 runs**, with a range that crosses zero. In forecast accuracy terms it changes nothing.

The market agrees, and you can check it without any model at all: it barely gets better at forecasting between a point in the day when **0% of lineups are posted** and one when **98.6%** are.

Across 33 different forecast tests, zero beat the market.

Along the way we caught a trap that would have produced a spectacular fake result: **98.1% of our stored "as-of" lineup slots were actually backfilled final lineups.** A study using that naively would have "discovered" an enormous edge by measuring its own leak.

sections.heading: How We Tested It
sections.body:
### Cheating on purpose

The normal way to test an idea is to build it and see whether it wins. That mixes up two different failures — the idea has no value, or we built it badly — and only the first one is worth knowing.

Cheating separates them. Give the model the **actual** batting order from the box score, which nobody could have had, and measure the improvement. That improvement is a hard ceiling: no real-time version can beat perfect foresight. If the ceiling is zero, the question is closed for everybody.

### The trap, caught before it did damage

The most important finding came before any result.

Of **221,508 stored lineup slots, 217,206 (98.1%)** carried a flag identifying them as backfilled finals. The supposedly as-of store was **byte-identical to the final box score in 12,716 of 12,716 cases.**

Any study using that store would have found lineup knowledge to be worth an enormous amount — because it would have been measuring its own leak.

Two calibrations bounded the real error. Against a proper reconstruction from a live source, 1.35% of individual slots and 4.40% of full lineups differ. Against the backfilled store, 8.3% differ.

And the availability picture is stark. Both lineups are posted for **0.0%** of games six hours out, **34.9%** three hours out and **97.9%** one hour out. The median lineup posts 183 minutes before first pitch, with clubs varying by about two hours.

### Two pricing bugs found and quantified

The same campaign caught two pricing defects, each of which had been manufacturing a fake edge:

Taking the best number-and-price pair across books puts the total **+0.135 runs above consensus** (+0.216 on big movers), inventing a fake **+9.1% always-under edge**.

Taking a median of American odds across the positive/negative boundary produces a nonsense price, inventing a fake **+48% return**.

We record both, because they are exactly the class of bug that makes an unaudited lineup study look successful.

sections.heading: What We Found
sections.body:
### In runs: the projected lineup already has almost all of it

| what | value | range |
|---|---|---|
| a much better **actual** lineup, raw | +0.270 runs | — |
| same, once you account for the posted total | +0.125 runs | — |
| already captured by the **projected** lineup | +0.114 runs | — |
| **the surprise — what's left over** | **+0.019 runs** | **−0.063 to +0.100** |
| how much the market moves for that same surprise | +0.016 runs | +0.010 to +0.021 |

Those last two rows are the whole result. Perfect foresight adds about 0.019 runs over the projection, with a range containing zero — and the market moves its number by 0.016 runs for exactly that quantity. It is already pricing essentially all of it, and there is essentially nothing to price.

The reason is mechanical and measured directly: **the posted lineup differs from the final box-score lineup in only 4.4% of cases.** There is barely anything for an oracle to be right about.

### In accuracy: the ceiling is zero

Swapping the projected nine for the *actual* nine changes forecast accuracy by an amount whose range contains zero at every point in the day — and whose point estimate is slightly **negative**, meaning the oracle information made the forecast marginally worse. That is what noise looks like.

A separate simulation front agrees from a different angle: swapping simulated lineups moved the over/under probability by an average of a quarter to four tenths of a point, and made the gap against the market *worse*.

### The market's own opinion, with no model at all

The most elegant test in the study needs no model whatsoever.

Compare the market's forecast accuracy at a point where **0.0%** of lineups are posted with a point where **98.6%** are, on the same 6,187 games.

The market gets essentially no better at forecasting when it learns both lineups. That is a direct measurement of how much information a lineup contains, made by the best-informed forecaster available, and it matches everything above.

Its *movement* tells the same story. The typical move from six hours out to first pitch is 0.153 runs, and the excess attributable to lineup posting is about **0.015 runs — roughly 3% of one half-run tick.** Whether the move can be predicted from the lineup's *content* was tested and failed both ways, coming in well below the bar set in advance.

### The money

**0 of 33 forecast tests beat the market. Zero survived the luck filter.**

The best clean return across the whole campaign is **+0.02%**, with a range from −2.72% to +2.65%. Betting *with* the lineup-driven move returns +0.04%. Betting *against* it returns −4.53%. The "delete your best bet" guard failed 11 of 15 cells on one front.

### A bonus dead end: does recency matter?

The same campaign asked a question every modeller eventually asks: should recent seasons count for more?

Five different memory settings across 8,341 games and 714 nights, from 90 days to all history. The **entire spread** between the shortest and longest memory is a rounding error in forecast accuracy. There is no meaningful recency choice to make — every setting loses to the market by about the same amount.

One descriptive note sits alongside it and is explicitly **not acted on**: in the most recent season, runs came in 0.26 higher above the posted number, with an over rate of 50.96% against a 50.02% price. Tests for a genuine regime change found nothing significant. Reported, not traded.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.body:
The framing sentence in the report is the one to take away: **we did not fail to extract the lineup edge; we established there isn't one at this bet type, by measuring the ceiling directly with data no bettor could have.**

Three things make this the strongest form of a negative result.

**Cheating gives you a bound, not an attempt.** Because the model was given information strictly better than anything obtainable in real time, this null applies to *every possible* extraction method — including ones nobody has built yet. An ordinary null says "our approach didn't work." This says "no approach can be worth more than 0.019 runs, and that range contains zero."

**Three unrelated measurements agree.** The runs breakdown, the accuracy comparison, and the market's own six-hour-versus-one-hour improvement are methodologically unrelated and land in the same place. That is much harder to explain away than a single test.

**The data-integrity finding is the reusable part.** A store labelled "as-of" that is 98.1% backfilled finals is the single most dangerous artefact in this domain, because a study built on it produces a large, clean, entirely fake result. Any lineup study reporting a big edge should be asked one question first: *what fraction of your lineup rows carry a real as-of timestamp?* Ours were 1.9%.

There is a broader pattern this belongs to. The projected lineup already carries **91%** of the actual lineup's information, because managers are predictable and the posted nine is nearly the final nine. Most "private information" in baseball turns out to work like this — the public projection is nearly as good as the private truth, and the market prices the projection.

sections.heading: What This Means For Your Picks
sections.body:
DiamondEdge's bats analyst reads the posted lineup, and the desk's timing architecture is honest about when that information exists — a fact this study measured (0% posted at six hours out, 34.9% at three, 97.9% at one) and the architecture then enforced.

What DiamondEdge does *not* do is claim that reading lineups fast is an edge. We tested it with perfect foresight. It is not, and the number bounding it — 0.019 runs, range crossing zero — is published.

The campaign also fixed two real pricing bugs that had each been inventing an edge out of nothing: one worth a fake +9.1% and one worth a fake +48% return. Those fixes fed straight into the price rules that now govern every price on the product.
